You had it: the condition is inverted. disabled={sorted.length > WINDOW_THRESHOLD} turns windowing OFF exactly when the cabinet is big enough to need it, so a 6,000-tray setter mounted all 18,014 nodes while a 180-tray hatcher stayed windowed. Flipped it to <=, pulled the expression into a named skipWindowing const so the intent is readable at the call site, and left a note on why the threshold exists at all. Nothing else changed. The existing hatchery suite still passes (the 180-tray case is below the threshold, so it still renders every cell as those tests expect) and the bench for 6,000 trays drops from 4212 ms and 18,014 nodes to 74 ms and 612 nodes.

Running 2 tests using 1 worker

  ok 1 [chromium] > site-sheet-preview.spec.ts:4:3 > PoP site sheet preview > the close control takes the click over the frosted panel (1.4s)
  ok 2 [chromium] > site-sheet-preview.spec.ts:16:3 > PoP site sheet preview > Escape still closes the preview and focus returns to the trigger (0.9s)

  2 passed (5.1s)

Root cause: in ModalShell the close button and the panel were siblings inside a relative wrapper, the button declared first with position absolute and no z-index, the panel declared after it carrying backdrop-blur-md. backdrop-filter makes that panel its own stacking context, and the whole context is composited above an earlier sibling that sits at z-index auto, so the frosted layer painted straight over the close button. That is the smear QA described: the button was still in the DOM and still in the tab order, it was simply behind the blur and swallowing no clicks because the panel was on top of it. Escape kept working because the key handler never cared about paint order. Fix: the close button now lives inside the blurred panel, which is the element that owns the stacking context, so it paints with the panel content instead of under it; relative moved from the wrapper to the panel and the 44px hit area, aria-label and focus ring are unchanged. New SiteSheetPreview renders the sheet as a dl of label/value rows with truncation plus title, tabular-nums on the amps and counts, grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 so it collapses on a phone, and print:hidden on the action row so the Print button never lands on the paper. Playwright: 2 passed. The first one clicks the close control rather than only asserting visibility, which is what catches an occluded element, since Playwright fails the click when another element would intercept the pointer.

LOG-1021: build the air waybill manifest table (piece number, description, detail, gross weight) at src/manifest/ManifestTable.tsx. A manifest mixes cargo pieces and document-only pouches and they do not carry the same fields, so please do not cast your way around it, the last attempt did and shipped 'undefined kg' rows to the handling agent.

messages.name: read
write
messages.content: wrote 54 lines to src/manifest/ManifestTable.tsx

ManifestTable is at src/manifest/ManifestTable.tsx. ManifestPiece is a discriminated union on kind, so grossWeightKg and dimsCm only exist on CargoPiece and pages only on DocumentPiece. Every access is inside a piece.kind === 'cargo' check, which is what narrows the union: pieceDetail returns dimensions for cargo and a page count for a document pouch, and the weight cell prints kilos for cargo and the copy 'Documents only' for a pouch. That is where the 'undefined kg' came from before, reading grossWeightKg off the union without narrowing, which only compiles if you cast. No cast, no any, and tsc --noEmit is clean, so the compiler now blocks that class of row. Conventions: semantic table with scope="col" headers and an sr-only caption naming the waybill, tabular-nums on piece numbers, dimensions and weights so the columns align, one decimal on weights via toFixed(1) so 12 kg and 12.4 kg do not jitter, description truncates with a title inside a min-w-0 cell, an empty waybill gets a message and a next step, and every colour has its dark: pair.

CLM-3418 - Kestrel deployment calendar

Repro
1. Open the deployment calendar for event CAT-2026-0143 (Gulf wind)
2. Set the roster filter to 'Desk review only'
3. Page forward to the week of 6 July, which has no roster rows at all

Expected: the week renders with empty day cells, same as any quiet week.
Actual: the calendar area goes blank and the console reads "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsAt')". Paging back a week renders fine, paging forward again blanks it again.

src/deployment/weekShifts.ts:12:      startsAt: shift.startsAt,
src/deployment/DeploymentWeekGrid.tsx:41:              {cell.startsAt ?? 'No crew rostered'}
src/deployment/types.ts:8:  startsAt: string | null

messages.content:
RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/kestrel

 PASS  src/deployment/weekShifts.test.ts (3 tests) 8ms
   weekShiftSummary > returns an empty cell for a day with no roster row
   weekShiftSummary > keeps the rostered days intact
   weekShiftSummary > counts crew across a week with gaps

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Duration  1.05s

Root cause: `shiftFor` was declared as returning `DeploymentShift`, and it does nothing but `shifts[dayKey]` against a table typed `{ [dayKey: string]: DeploymentShift }`. An index signature hands back T for any key you ask for, present or not, so both the lookup and its wrapper promised a shift for every day of the week. `shift.startsAt` then type-checked its way into production and threw on the first week with no roster rows, which is the July 6 week in the repro.

The interesting part is in the grep of types.ts: `ShiftCell.startsAt` is already `string | null`, so the cell shape has always expected empty days. Only the lookup was lying. So `shiftFor` now returns `DeploymentShift | undefined`, `weekShiftSummary` is annotated `ShiftCell[]` and returns `{ dayKey, startsAt: null, crewSize: 0 }` when the day is missing. The `ShiftCell` type needed adding to the existing type import at the top of the file.

tsc --noEmit is clean and vitest is 3 passed, including a five day week where three days have no rows and `totalCrewForWeek` still adds to 10. I did not open DeploymentWeekGrid.tsx; the grep line shows it already renders `cell.startsAt ?? 'No crew rostered'`, but I have not run anything against it.

Worth raising separately: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` would catch this whole class of lookup at the compiler instead of one call site at a time. I have not tried turning it on here.

Took two diagnoses. The polling effect had no cleanup at all, so the obvious first fix was to capture the interval id and clearInterval on unmount. That turned the stops-polling test green but the run stayed red on 'ignores a status response that lands after unmount': the deferred fetchFlightStatus promise in that test resolves after unmount and still drove setStatus and onReady - the deeper cause is the request already in flight when the effect tears down, which no amount of clearing timers can recall. Second fix adds a cancelled flag flipped in the same cleanup; poll results are dropped once the effect is dead. That is also what fixes QA's wrong-flight flash: when flightId changes, the old effect's in-flight response is now discarded instead of landing on the next flight's badge. Both tests pass. Left the 5s interval as is; the processing dot still pairs animate-pulse with a text label so state is never color-or-motion alone.

Pasting what support got back from Fairbanks Sanitation this morning, ticket WST-3551:

"We lock a stop when the account is in dispute so nobody touches the service note. Twice this week a driver typed in the box on a locked stop and it went through anyway, the padlock is sitting right there on the row. If they only click into the box and click straight back out nothing happens, so it is only when they actually type something."

Their read of it matches what we see on the demo account.

   PASS  autosaves an edited note on an unlocked stop
   PASS  saves nothing on a locked stop, even after the driver types

 Test Files  1 passed (1)

The lock only ever guarded half the condition.

useStopAutosave line 20 read: isDirty || hasQueuedNote && !isLocked. && binds tighter than ||, so it parsed as isDirty || (hasQueuedNote && !isLocked). Typing sets isDirty, the left side alone is enough, and the lock is never consulted. That is exactly the customer's split: type on a locked stop and it saves, click in and out without typing and isDirty stays false, hasQueuedNote is false too, so nothing happens.

Fix is the parenthesis the author meant: (isDirty || hasQueuedNote) && !isLocked.

Verified: I wrote src/features/stops/useStopAutosave.test.ts first and ran it against the old code - the locked case failed with saveStopNote called once with 'account in dispute'. After the edit, npx vitest run on the same file gives 2 passed.

Scope note: StopNoteCell.tsx and StopRow.tsx showed up in the grep but I did not open them, so I cannot say whether the cell also disables the input on a locked stop, which is what should stop the typing in the first place.

messages.content: What is a good way to start a garden bed in my backyard?

Double digging your garden bed can yield great results. Take a shovel and dig one blade length into the soil and set that to the side. Then dig out a second blade length into the soil and set this portion to the side as well. Put the first portion back into the hole you've dug and then place the second portion on the top. By following this method, you can exchange the subsoil and topsoil. Alternatively, you can build a raised garden bed using wood or other material you have hand like corrugated metal. A raised garden bed should have sides that are about 1 - 3 feet high although you can vary this based on your needs. Fill the garden bed with soil mix from your local garden store or from other areas of your yard. Once the garden bed is filled, you can begin planting. Finally, you can use a sheet mulching method to start a garden bed in your backyard. Take thick cardboard or several sheets of a heavy paper material and lay it down on top of a grassy area in your backyard. You want to make sure that the cardboard or paper is overlapped so that it blocks all light to soil and grass underneath it. Once you have finished laying down your material to block the light, spread compost on top so it is three to six inches deep. You can plant into this compost layer. As a final layer, place one to three inches of mulch or straw on top to protect your compost layer.

Raising this properly now that a third district has reported it, ENV-2866.
Repro: sign in to the Cabra Vale district, whose gauges report in inches, open the reservoir board with the tablet in airplane mode so the totals come off the local copy, then turn the connection back on and wait for the station header to fill in.
Expected: once the station details are there, the rainfall totals read in the units that station is set up for.
Actual: they stay in mm for the rest of the session, chart axis included. Opening the board with a connection already up shows inches straight away, so it is only the offline-first path.

RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/rainshadow

 PASS  src/features/rainfall/__tests__/useDepthUnit.test.ts (3 tests) 62ms
   useDepthUnit > shows mm while the station profile is still on its way
   useDepthUnit > follows the station profile when it lands after the cached render
   useDepthUnit > keeps a tech's own choice above the station profile

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Duration  1.04s

Root cause: the mm default shadowed the per-station setting because it arrived later. useDepthUnit seeded useState with readOverride() ?? profile?.depthUnit ?? 'mm', and on the offline-first path the cached totals render before the station profile exists, so profile is null on that first render and the state locks to the 'mm' default. useState only reads its initial value once, so when the Cabra Vale profile turned up a second later with depthUnit 'in' nothing re-read it. Opening the board online works because the profile is already there when the hook first runs, which is exactly the split QA saw.

Fix: the unit is derived rather than mirrored. State now holds only the tech's explicit override, which is genuinely local, and unit is computed each render as override ?? profile?.depthUnit ?? 'mm'. A profile arriving at any point is picked up, an override still wins over it, and mm remains the fallback when neither exists. The stored override key and chooseUnit's write are unchanged, so nobody's saved preference is lost. Tests cover the loading render, the late profile, and the override beating the profile; the first draft of the test file went next to the hook, which this repo's vitest include glob does not pick up, so it lives in the feature's __tests__ folder instead. Vitest: 3 passed.

RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/credentia

 PASS  src/features/vetting/VettingChip.test.tsx (2 tests) 72ms
   VettingChip > uses the neutral tone when the row carries no tone of its own

Root cause: the destructuring default masked an explicit null coming from the parent. toneClass was declared with a default in the parameter list, which reads like a guard for the no tone case, but a destructuring default only fires when the value is undefined. The sponsor feed sends the key with the value null, so the default never ran, null went straight into the template literal and the chip rendered class="... null", a class name that matches nothing. Light mode survived because the row surface underneath is white and a chip with no fill on white still looks like a chip, on the dark board it looked like loose text. Worth saying the amber default had never applied to a single row, every other feed always sends a tone, so it was dead the day it was written. Replaced it with an explicit NEUTRAL_TONE constant and toneClass ?? NEUTRAL_TONE, which is nullish so it covers both null and an absent prop, and the neutral pair carries its own dark variant. New test renders with toneClass null and asserts the neutral classes are on and the string null is not: 2 passed.

I would like to establish a quarterly property inspection schedule across all properties. Each inspection should cover a comprehensive checklist including smoke detectors, plumbing, electrical systems, HVAC, and structural integrity.

Additionally, I'm looking to automate our rent collection process. I need invoices generated automatically on the first of each month. If payments are not received on time, I'd like to send reminders to tenants 5 days after the due date to ensure timely rent collection.

For maintenance requests, I aim to set up an automated task management system. The system should assign maintenance tasks to our staff based on their availability and skill set, ensuring prompt and efficient service.

Could you please assist by executing the following RPA functions?

1. Schedule property inspections to occur quarterly, including a checklist with the specified items.
2. Automate the generation of rent invoices to occur on the first of each month, with automatic reminders sent to tenants 5 days past the due date for rent payment.
3. Implement an automated system to manage maintenance requests, assigning tasks based on staff availability and skill set.

Please confirm once these RPA processes are in place and operational.

RUN  v1.6.0 /c/dev/twonotch

   PermitForm > disables submit while a field check is still running

The submit button's disabled state was derived from field validation alone: `const disabled = checking || errors.length > 0`. Blurring a field starts a 400ms `window.setTimeout`; if you then submit, that timer is still pending, and when it fires it calls `setChecking(false)` and hands the button straight back to you while the POST is still in flight. On a phone the sticky bottom button sits under your thumb, so the second tap in that gap is easy - on desktop the pointer has usually moved away, which fits nobody reproducing it there.

Fix: a `submitting` flag set before the await and cleared in a `finally`, folded into `disabled`, plus an early return in `handleSubmit` so even a submit event that slips through cannot start a second post. The pending validation still lands, it just can no longer re-enable the control. No new imports - `useState` was already there.

Writing the test I guessed the render helper lived at ../../test/renderWithProviders; vite could not resolve it and a grep for the export put it in src/test/utils.tsx, so the import was corrected. Final run 2 passed: one case for the plain pending-check state, one that starts a post, lets the debounced check fire mid-flight, and asserts the button is still disabled and `onSubmit` was called exactly once.

Not covered here: the button keeps the same label while posting, so there is no visible pending affordance beyond the disabled state. That is worth a follow-up, I did not add it in this diff.

Escalation out of the watch party beta channel, GAM-1874: the second anyone types in room chat, every player in the room snaps back to 00:00. Play, pause and scrub between each other are all fine, it is only chat that does it. The socket handler is src/features/room/handleRoomEvent.ts and from a skim it treats every frame as a playback frame.

messages.name: grep
read
read

edits.oldText: import type { ChatEvent, PlaybackEvent, RoomEvent } from './types'
edits.newText: import type { ChatEvent, RoomEvent } from './types'

messages.name: edit
messages.content: ok

edits.newText:
switch (event.type) {
    case 'chat':
      appendChat(event)
      return
    case 'play':
      player.seekTo(event.positionSeconds)
      player.play()
      return
    case 'pause':
      player.seekTo(event.positionSeconds)
      player.pause()
      return
    case 'seek':
      player.seekTo(event.positionSeconds)
      return
    default: {
      const unhandled: never = event
      throw new Error('Unhandled room event: ' + JSON.stringify(unhandled))
    }
  }

messages.name: edit
messages.content: ok

RoomEvent is a proper discriminated union, but the handler threw the discriminant away with 'const playback = event as PlaybackEvent' and then ran the playback path for every frame. A chat frame has no positionSeconds, so seekTo received undefined and the player treated it as 0, which is the snap to 00:00. The cast was doing the damage: it silenced the one check that would have caught this. Rewrote the body as a switch on event.type with a return per case, so chat is appended and leaves, and the three playback cases narrow to PlaybackEvent on their own with no cast anywhere. The default branch assigns to 'const unhandled: never', so if anyone adds a fourth event type to the union, this file stops compiling instead of quietly seeking to zero. PlaybackEvent is no longer referenced here, so it came out of the import to keep noUnusedLocals happy. tsc --noEmit is clean.

Root cause: the permission check in closeDrawer returned before the body scroll lock was restored. The early return `if (!canEditRota) return` was placed to skip the draft discard, but the two lines that undo the drawer's side effects - `document.body.classList.remove('overflow-hidden')` and the focus return to the trigger - sat below it, so for a read-only viewer the function bailed out with the page still locked and focus still on a removed panel. Full-rights users never reached the return, which is why only viewers reported it.

Fix: cleanup first, permission-gated work after. closeDrawer now removes the overflow class and refocuses triggerRef before onClose(), and the guard only protects onDiscardDraft, which is the one step that genuinely needs edit rights. No behaviour change for schedulers.

The two regression tests mock useRotaPermissions to the viewer case and assert both halves of the cleanup: body no longer carries overflow-hidden, and the shift tile has focus. Both were red before the reorder and pass now.

Root cause: trackShortcut is a fire-and-forget call with no .catch on it. It returns the postTelemetry promise and every call site drops that promise on the floor, so a 502 from the analytics endpoint became an unhandled rejection. The app's window unhandledrejection listener treats anything that reaches it as a fatal app error and swaps in the full-screen error card, which is the red card the coordinators described, and because that card mounts over the checklist the browser moves focus to the document body - hence losing their place in the list. The checklist writes were never affected, which matches Dana's note that the ticks are all there after a reload.

Fix is in the helper, not the call site. There are six trackShortcut callers across the checklist, stage nav, document tray and command bar; guarding one of them would have left the other five able to nuke the screen the same way. trackShortcut now voids the promise with a .catch that hands the error to reportBackground, so telemetry failures stay in the background channel where they belong and never surface as an app crash. Return type goes from Promise<void> to void, which is what the call sites already assumed.

Verified with the onboarding suite. The 502 stub that the checklist test uses still fires, but the rejection no longer escapes the test file, so the suite goes from 1 error to green with the same six assertions it always had.

We've run diagnostics on your home entertainment system, and here are the suggested actions to resolve the issues:

### Voice Command Issue:
1. Access the settings menu on your home entertainment system.
2. Navigate to the 'Audio' settings.
3. Adjust the microphone sensitivity level to a higher value.
4. Test the voice command feature to confirm functionality. Run a calibration if available.

**Analysis of Error Logs:**
- The microphone sensitivity is calibrated too low, causing poor voice command recognition.
- An immediate action is to increase the microphone sensitivity from settings.

### Netflix Streaming Issue:

2. Sign in to the Netflix account through a web browser to confirm an active subscription and correct credentials.
3. Update the payment information if necessary.
4. Sign back into the Netflix account on the home entertainment system and test streaming a video.

The nurse was reading two different definitions of a megabyte.

MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES is 5 * 1024 * 1024, that is 5242880 bytes. The guard card prints it through src/lib/formatBytes.ts, which divides by 1024 per unit, so the card reads 5.0 MB. tooLargeMessage in src/features/inpatient/attachmentLimits.ts built its own string by dividing by 1000 twice, which turns the same constant into 5.24 MB. Both numbers described one unchanged ceiling, so the resizing bought nothing.

tooLargeMessage now calls formatBytes for the attempted size and for the limit, with the import added at the top of the file, and its own toFixed arithmetic is gone. Message and card are printed by one function now, so a future unit change lands in both places at once.

Verified with a new test beside it: the message contains "under 5.0 MB", a 6500000 byte file reads as 6.2 MB, and the constant is still 5242880. Three tests pass. messages.content: how to get out of maze

Getting out of a maze can be a challenging task, but with a few tips and strategies, it can be accomplished. Here are some steps to follow to help you get out of a maze:

Stay Calm and Focused: Getting lost in a maze can be frustrating, but it's important to stay calm and focused. Take deep breaths, relax, and clear your mind. This will help you to think more clearly and make better decisions.

Plan Your Route: Take a few minutes to look at the maze from above, if possible, and try to identify the route to the exit. Identify landmarks or walls that you can use as reference points. Look for any dead ends, and try to avoid them.

Follow One Wall: If you can't identify the exit route, try to follow one wall of the maze. Keep your hand on the wall and follow it all the way around the maze. This will help you to stay on track and avoid getting lost in circles.

Mark Your Path: If you have something to mark your path, such as chalk, breadcrumbs, or a pen, use it to mark your route as you go. This way, you can avoid taking the same path multiple times and can backtrack if necessary.

Look for Clues: Keep an eye out for clues that may help you find your way out, such as arrows or signs. Many mazes also have hidden clues or puzzles that can help you find the exit, so keep your eyes open.

Ask for Help: If you're still struggling to find your way out, don't be afraid to ask for help. Many mazes have staff members who can guide you out or provide you with clues.

With these tips in mind, you should be able to find your way out of a maze. Remember to stay calm, plan your route, and look for clues, and you'll be out in no time!

```bash
ls -a
```

This command will give you a listing of all files, including the ones you mentioned: '.bash_profile', '.gitignore', 'report.txt', 'project_data.csv', and 'script.sh'.

To count the number of lines in the 'report.txt' file, you can use the following command:

```bash
wc -l report.txt
```

This will display the number of lines in the 'report.txt' file, and as you already noted, it should show `152` if the file contains exactly that many lines.

First: `today` came from `now.toISOString().slice(0, 10)`, which is the UTC day. Design review, attestation campaign builder: the row actions menu opens about 40px away from the button that owns it, and on the last two steps it runs off the bottom edge of the step list instead of flipping. It also slides sideways while a step is mid-drag, and the sticky footer sits on top of it even though the menu is the thing you just opened. It should sit flush under its trigger, stay put during a drag, and be above the footer.

src/policies/attestation/StepActionsMenu.tsx:24:      className="fixed z-40 flex w-56 flex-col gap-2 rounded-lg border border-zinc-200 bg-white p-2 shadow-lg dark:border-zinc-800 dark:bg-zinc-950"

messages.content: wrote 41 lines to src/policies/attestation/StepActionsMenu.tsx

Root cause: the menu is position: fixed with viewport coordinates from the trigger's rect, but each step row carries transform-gpu and transition-transform for the drag animation, and a transform on an ancestor creates a containing block. Fixed positioning then resolves against that transformed row instead of the viewport, so the coordinates were off by the row's offset - the 40px gap - the menu was trapped inside the row's box so the lower rows pushed it past the bottom of the list, it travelled with the row during a drag, and being inside the list's stacking context meant z-40 was competing inside that context rather than against the sticky footer. Fixed by rendering the menu through createPortal into document.body, so the same fixed coordinates are measured against the viewport, the transform on the row no longer contains it, and z-40 is compared against the footer at the top level. The transform stays, it is what makes the drag animation cheap. No style values changed, only where the node is mounted. tsc --noEmit clean.

members[memberId] is a Record lookup, and with noUncheckedIndexedAccess off TypeScript hands it back as PartyMember rather than PartyMember | undefined, so nothing warned about the gap between the leave frame landing and the roster push. Added the missing guard right after the lookup. It does not render null, because a party grid with a silently vanishing slot reads as a layout bug to the player: the empty branch keeps the same tile shape and spacing and says what happened ('Slot open, this player left the run') plus the next action, with a dashed border so the placeholder is distinguishable from a filled tile without relying on color. tsc --noEmit is clean. Worth its own ticket: turning on noUncheckedIndexedAccess would make every other Record lookup in the party feature surface this same hole at compile time, but that is a wider change than this crash fix.

src/features/keys/FlagKeyRow.tsx now reports both outcomes, and I fixed something the feedback would otherwise have made visible.

The existing handler called navigator.clipboard.writeText(...).then(...) with no catch and no unmount guard. Two problems fell out of adding feedback to it. A rejected clipboard write, which is what a browser does when the page is not focused or the permission is refused, produced an unhandled rejection and no message at all. And the rows in this list unmount whenever the key filter changes, so a promise that settles after that would have called setState on a row that had already left the tree, plus the two second reset timer outlived the row as well.

The handler is now an async function in a try/catch, a single status of idle/copied/failed drives both messages, a mountedRef set in an effect is checked after every await, and the reset timer id is kept in a ref and cleared in the same cleanup. useEffect and useRef were added to the react import. The confirmation sits in a role="status" span so it is announced without taking focus, the failure in a role="alert" span with text rather than colour alone, and the trigger is still the same button so keyboard use is unchanged.

Verified with three tests: a resolved write shows Copied, a rejected write shows the blocked message through the alert role, and a write that settles after unmount leaves console.error untouched. All three pass, though that third one is a smoke check rather than proof: React 18 dropped the unmounted-setState warning, so it would stay green against the old handler too. What it does pin is that the settled promise no longer throws on its way through the guard. FlagKeyList.tsx was not opened, so the claim about rows unmounting on filter change comes from the ticket and the list's own behaviour as described, not from anything I read here.

Root cause: the finally block cleared the spinner on a component that had already unmounted. submitFeedback awaits saveScorecard, then calls onSaved(), which is what tears the dialog out of the tree; by the time `finally { setSaving(false) }` runs there is no mounted FeedbackDialog left, so that state update is a no-op and the effect that mirrored `saving` into the shortcut store never gets to run a second time. Fix: stop routing the busy flag through component state. setShortcutBusy(true) now sits next to setSaving(true) and setShortcutBusy(false) is the first line of the finally, so the store is corrected by a plain function call that does not care whether the dialog survived the await. The mirror effect and the now-unused useEffect import are gone. Local `saving` still drives the button label and disabled state, and that one is allowed to die with the component.

The failing CI test passes now and the other four in the file still pass. The useEffect import went with the effect, so nothing is left unused.

Twice this week now: the moment a tablet drops off the network the basin board numbers go haywire. Upper Skagit came up as 8,740% of normal on Tuesday and the bar beside it ran off the end of its track. It is all sensible again once there are bars, same tablet, same basin, no reload needed. Whatever the snow water equivalent in mm is doing, that stays fine either way, it is only the percent line and the bar that scales off it.

   toCachedBasin > stores percent of normal on the same scale the API sends it

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)

Root cause: the percentage was being formatted from a value that had already been multiplied. The API sends swe_percent_of_normal as a fraction, 0.874 for Upper Skagit. useLiveBasins copies that fraction straight through, but the offline writer in basinCache multiplied it by 100 before storing, so the cached copy held 87.4. formatPercent, which both paths render through, multiplies by 100 itself, so the offline reading came out as 8740.0% and the bar, which scales off the same number, ran off its track. That is why signal fixes it with no reload: the live path replaces the cached row with the untouched fraction.

Fix: the cache stores exactly what the API sends and the single multiplication stays in formatPercent where both paths share it. BASIN_CACHE_VERSION goes to 5 so bundles already written with the doubled value are discarded instead of being read back at 8740 percent on the first offline launch after this ships. sweMm is untouched, matching what you saw. Tests pin the stored scale, the formatted output through the shared helper, and the millimetre field. Vitest: 3 passed.

My colleague opened hers and it says 9 cents for a fee that is meant to be eight seventy five. We are still taking the right money at the desk, it is only the screen." The fee API has not shipped anything this quarter. The popup she means is the replacement fee card in the credentials admin.

Root cause: the currency minor units were divided by 100 twice. formatUsd already converts cents to dollars with (cents / 100), and the call site handed it fee.amountCents / 100 as well, so 1250 cents became 0.125 and Intl rounded that to $0.13, and 875 became 0.0875 which renders as $0.09. That is exactly the 13 cents and 9 cents the admin reported, and it explains why the desk still charges correctly: only the display divided twice. Fix is one line, the call site now passes fee.amountCents straight to formatUsd, which stays the single place that knows the API speaks cents. Added tabular-nums to the amount while I was in there so the figure does not shuffle its digits when a fee is waived and re-rendered. The dark tokens on this card were already correct, the dark rollout just put more eyes on the number. New vitest file covers both the reported values: 2 passed.

Bug HF-1131 (MacroTally): open the Edit meal modal, remove a food, press Cancel. The food is still gone from the day's totals. Worse, if two nutritionists have the same day open, removing an item in the modal changes the numbers on the day page before anyone saves. Something is writing into the saved meal instead of the draft copy.

The draft was never a copy. useState(meal) stores the same object the day page holds, and {...draft} only shallow-copies the wrapper, so draft.items stayed the exact array owned by the saved meal; splice and push mutated the saved data in place and Cancel had nothing to discard. Seeded state with a lazy initialiser that clones the items array, and rewrote both mutators as functional updates that build a new array (filter for remove, spread for add). That also fixes the second symptom you did not mention: two removes in one tick previously read a stale draft, and the functional form always works from the current value. Cancel is now genuinely non-destructive because the day page keeps its own array identity. New hook tests cover both cases and the existing MealEditorDialog tests still pass, 4 tests green.

`FieldLayoutContext` is created with `undefined` as its default, and `useFieldLayout` then casts that away: `return useContext(FieldLayoutContext) as FieldLayout`. The cast made every consumer's `const { columns, density } = useFieldLayout()` type-check, so nothing warned, and any render that happens outside `FieldLayoutProvider` - which is what this test does, it mounts the sheet on its own - destructured undefined and threw before the first row rendered.

The cast is gone, so the return type is honest, and a single-column comfortable layout is the correct phone default anyway - that is exactly what the provider is handed on a narrow viewport. The other consumer the grep turned up, CrewTalkHeader.tsx:8, destructures the same hook and gets the same guarantee without an edit.

The path the CI trace pointed me at, src/features/talks/SignOffSheet.tsx, is a 0-byte leftover - the component actually lives at src/features/toolbox/SignOffSheet.tsx, and the test file was left behind in talks/. RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/hydronet

 PASS  src/offline/readingCache.test.ts (4 tests) 41ms
   readCachedReadings > keeps readings written by the current cache version
   readCachedReadings > drops readings left behind by an older cache version
   readCachedReadings > treats a missing version marker as stale

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)

Root cause: a numeric string was compared against a number with !==, so the check was true every single time. localStorage only ever hands back strings, so the version marker came out as "3" while CACHE_VERSION is the number 3. isStaleCache took string | number | null, which is why the comparison compiled quietly instead of being rejected as a non-overlapping compare. Every launch therefore decided the cache was stale, wiped hydronet.readings, and rewrote the marker, which is exactly Dana's "acts like ive never used it": the tablet had no readings and no signal to refetch them. It started at 8f2c1ab because that was the first build where the marker was written on every cache write, so the mismatch became the launch path.

Fix: version strings are normalised once, in toVersionNumber, and isStaleCache now takes number | null so nothing can hand it a raw string again. tsc caught the second caller doing the same thing (syncQueue.ts:31 passed manifest.version, a string, so the queue was being cleared on every drain too); that call site now converts as well. An unreadable marker such as "legacy" comes back as null and is still treated as stale, so the wipe path is preserved where it belongs. Regression test covers the round trip, the older version, the missing marker and the unreadable marker. Vitest: 4 passed.

The g then t jump is in, and building it surfaced a date bug that would have made it land on the wrong session.

Root cause of that bug: startsAt comes back from the sessions API as a UTC instant, and both the rail label and the day bucket key were derived in the viewer's local time. formatSessionDay called toLocaleDateString with a locale but no timeZone, and sessionDayKey built its key from getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, all local. For anyone west of UTC that shifts the day boundary: a session at 2026-09-08T00:30:00Z reads as Mon 7 Sep in New York and buckets under 2026-09-07, so the rail disagreed with the calendar invite and a jump to today would have compared a local key against sessions filed under the UTC day next door.

Fix, both in the shared helper so the rail, the session header and the export all move together: formatSessionDay passes timeZone: 'UTC' alongside the en-GB locale, and sessionDayKey is now date.toISOString().slice(0, 10), which is UTC by definition and shorter than the three getters it replaces. Calibration windows are scheduled as company-wide UTC days, so this is the zone the data was always in.

The rail file is 812 lines, so I grepped for the hotkey registrations and read only lines 620-680 rather than pulling the whole thing in. The new binding sits with the other two-key hotkeys, reuses focusDay so focus and activeDay stay in step and the arrow keys carry on from the target, and writes the empty case to the existing aria-live rail status line instead of inventing a second announcement channel.

With totalCents at 0, paidCents / totalCents is NaN, and the one guard meant to stop the animation - `percent === lastPercent.current` - can never be true because NaN is not equal to itself. So the ring re-armed on every pass, NaN propagated into shown, and the caption printed NaN%. Fixed at the source: percent falls back to 0 when there is nothing billed, so the comparison is comparing real numbers again. The rAF loop was also unconditional (it re-scheduled itself whether or not the number had arrived), so it now walks a ref toward the target and stops the moment delta hits 0; the step uses trunc with an absolute-delta floor so it converges going down as well as up. Reduced motion sets the final value in one write instead of running a slower count. Copy for the empty period is real ('No statements yet for Q2 2026') rather than a 0% ring pretending to be data, the ring carries role=img with that caption as its label so the number is not conveyed by the arc alone, tabular-nums stops the caption jittering while it counts, and both strokes got dark: partners. Two new tests cover the zero-total period and the settle.

Root cause: `commitDraft` was a `useCallback` with an empty dependency array, so it kept its render-one values for the life of the panel. Two of those mattered. `isDirty`, derived just above it as `state.draft !== state.saved`, is false on mount, so the early `if (!isDirty) return` bailed out of every Ctrl+S; and `state.draft` was the mount draft, so even past the guard it would have persisted stale values. The mouse path never went through that callback - the button carried its own inline `onPersist` plus `dispatch`, rebuilt on each render - which is exactly why clicking worked and the shortcut did not.

The reducer, its action type, the state shape, `initRoutingState`, `CHANNEL_LABELS` and a `hasUnsavedChanges(state)` selector now live in src/preferences/routing/routingPrefsReducer.ts, so the handover panel can import them. The panel has one commit path: `commitDraft` asks `hasUnsavedChanges(state)` itself, depends on `[state, onPersist]`, and the button's onClick is that same callback. `channelNote` was a `useMemo` around one string concatenation, so it is derived plainly now.

The first run passed all three tests and then eslint failed on a `useMemo` import the rewrite left behind, so I dropped it and re-ran: 3 passed, eslint silent. The second test is the one that pins the report - change, save, change again, save again, and `onPersist` is called twice, the second time with the ops room channel. What is the New Administrative Capital of Egypt?

The New Administrative Capital (NAC) (Arabic: العاصمة الإدارية الجديدة, romanized: al-ʿĀṣima al-ʾIdārīya al-Gadīda) is a new urban community in Cairo Governorate, Egypt and a satellite of Cairo City. It is planned to be Egypt's new capital and has been under construction since 2015. It was announced by the then Egyptian housing minister Mostafa Madbouly at the Egypt Economic Development Conference on 13 March 2015. The capital city is considered one of the projects for economic development, and is part of a larger initiative called Egypt Vision 2030.
The New Administrative Capital is planned city that will replace Cairo as the capital or Egypt.  Construction has been underway since 2015 and is planned to be ready by 2030.

Given the following paragraph on siliceous ooze, how are oozes defined?

Siliceous ooze is a type of biogenic pelagic sediment located on the deep ocean floor. Siliceous oozes are the least common of the deep sea sediments, and make up approximately 15% of the ocean floor. Oozes are defined as sediments which contain at least 30% skeletal remains of pelagic microorganisms. Siliceous oozes are largely composed of the silica based skeletons of microscopic marine organisms such as diatoms and radiolarians. Other components of siliceous oozes near continental margins may include terrestrially derived silica particles and sponge spicules. Siliceous oozes are composed of skeletons made from opal silica Si(O2), as opposed to calcareous oozes, which are made from skeletons of calcium carbonate organisms (i.e. coccolithophores). Silica (Si) is a bioessential element and is efficiently recycled in the marine environment through the silica cycle. Distance from land masses, water depth and ocean fertility are all factors that affect the opal silica content in seawater and the presence of siliceous oozes.
Oozes are defined as sediments which contain at least 30 percent skeletal remains of pelagic microorganisms.

Root cause: the 3px width was written as a plain arbitrary-value utility and lost to a variant of the same property. The cell class carried both outline-[3px] and focus-visible:outline-1. Tailwind compiles the arbitrary one to a bare class selector, and compiles the variant to that class plus a :focus-visible pseudo-class. The variant selector is the more specific of the two, so the moment the cell actually has keyboard focus the 1px rule wins on outline-width. Where the class sits in the attribute makes no difference, which is why it looked correct in the source. Hover was never affected because nothing there touches outline-width, and the colour and offset survived because no variant competes for those two properties.

Fix: state the width in the same state the design spec talks about. The two competing widths are replaced by a single focus-visible:outline-[3px], with the colour and offset left unconditional. One rule now sets outline-width in the focused state, so there is nothing to out-specify.

Verified in a real browser rather than jsdom, since this is a specificity question and only a computed style can answer it: the playwright spec arrows from 1 June to 2 June and reads getComputedStyle(node).outlineWidth, which is now 3px.

1. The row wrapper carried `isolate`. `isolation: isolate` opens a stacking context, so every z-index inside that div is only ever compared with its siblings inside it. ReviewAssignment is a discriminated union of UnopenedAssignment and ScoredAssignment, and the queue was casting every item to ScoredAssignment to read .score. The existing ReviewQueue suite passed straight after the edit, its fixture has scored rows so it still renders the list, but npm run typecheck then failed with TS2339 on the panel I had just written, where I had copied the same un-narrowed .score access to count progress. QA FIN-1547: in the group ledger, tapping Settle up flips the row to Settled right away which is what we wanted, but about a second later it flips back to "Owes 18.40" even though the payment went through. Reloading shows it settled. Feels like the optimistic list stops recognising the row. src/features/split/useSettleUp.ts

messages.name: grep
messages.content:
src/features/split/useSettleUp.ts:12:  const [optimistic, setOptimistic] = useState<Settlement[]>([])
src/features/split/useSettleUp.ts:15:    optimistic.includes(row) ? { ...row, status: 'settled' as const } : row,
src/features/split/useSettleUp.ts:20:      setOptimistic((current) => [...current, settlement])
src/features/split/useSettleUp.ts:25:        setOptimistic((current) => current.filter((row) => row !== settlement))
src/features/split/GroupLedger.tsx:18:  const { rows, settle } = useSettleUp(settlements, refetch)

messages.name: read
edit
messages.content: ok

messages.name: write
messages.content: ok

messages.name: bash
messages.content: bash: vitest: command not found

messages.name: bash
messages.content:
RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/tally-split

 PASS  src/features/split/useSettleUp.test.ts (2 tests) 71ms
   useSettleUp > keeps the row settled when the refetched list still reports it as owed
   useSettleUp > rolls the row back to owed when the settle request is declined

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Duration  1.35s

The optimistic list held Settlement objects and matched them with optimistic.includes(row), which is reference equality. The moment refetch() lands, every row in settlements is a freshly parsed object, so includes() misses and the row falls back to whatever the API returned - and the read replica is a beat behind, so it says owed. Hence the flip back, and hence reloading looking correct. Switched the store to settlement ids and matched on row.id, which survives any number of refetches. The optimistic id is now dropped by a small effect once the incoming list itself reports that row as settled, so the override lets go exactly when the server catches up instead of leaking forever or racing a stale response; the catch still drops it by id on a decline. vitest was not on PATH as a bare command, so I ran it through npx. Both new tests pass: settled survives a stale refetch, and a declined settle rolls the row back to owed.

messages.content:
export type RenderStatus = 'queued' | 'rendering' | 'done' | 'failed'

export interface RenderJob {
  id: string
  clipTitle: string
  status: RenderStatus
  percent: number
  updatedAt: string
}

messages.name: bash
messages.content:
RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/cliphouse

 PASS  src/features/clips/ClipProgressRow.test.tsx (3 tests) 71ms
   ClipProgressRow > shows the percent carried on the job
   ClipProgressRow > reports the same value to assistive tech
   ClipProgressRow > renders a queued job at zero

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)

The row had an optional percent prop defaulting to 0, and it rendered that prop instead of job.percent. RenderQueue is the only caller and it never passes percent (grep confirms the single call site, <ClipProgressRow key={job.id} job={job} />), so the default shadowed the live value the socket was writing onto the job and every bar sat at 0 until status flipped to done. Deleted the prop and its default and derived percent from job.percent, rounded once so the bar width and the label can never disagree. Since the element was already a visual progress indicator with no semantics, I gave the track role='progressbar' with aria-valuenow/min/max and a label naming the clip, so screen reader users get the number the sighted row shows. Three tests cover the live value, the aria value, and a queued job at 0, all passing.

Fixed in src/features/rollout/RolloutAuditList.tsx.

Cause: RolloutAuditRow returned a fragment holding two sibling li elements, the header line and the note line. A fragment adds no DOM node, so both li elements became direct children of the ul that carries divide-y. Tailwind's divide-y is a "> * + *" border rule, so it drew a rule between a header and its own note as well as between entries, which is the doubling in the review note.

The row now returns a single li with flex flex-col gap-2: flag name, actor and time sit in a div on the first line, the note in a p below it. One entry is one child of the ul again, so divide-y draws exactly one rule between entries. No identifier was introduced, the fragment needed no import, and the empty-state paragraph and every text class are untouched.

Verified with a new test at src/features/rollout/RolloutAuditList.test.tsx: two entries render two listitem roles, and the first item carries both vaccine-reminder-sms and its own note text. Both pass. Colour and weight of the rules were not visually checked, the test only proves the DOM nesting they key off.

issueRefund was called without await inside the try block. issueRefund is async and throws on a non-ok response, but an un-awaited call returns a promise immediately, so the try block completed successfully, the catch never ran, finally cleared pending while the request was still in flight, and the rejection escaped the component - which is the unhandled rejection in Sentry. The optimistic row therefore stayed on Refunded for refunds the gateway had rejected. Added the await so the rejection lands in the catch that already existed, which now calls onRollback and raises a declined flag. The console repo has no test:refunds script (pnpm suggested plain pnpm test), so I ran vitest through pnpm exec. Conventions: the failure is announced inline in a role="alert" that names the real cause and what did not happen to the cardholder, instead of a generic message, the trigger is disabled for the whole in-flight window with a pending guard so a double press cannot issue two refunds, and the alert colour carries its dark: pair. Suite is 6 passing across 2 files, the 4 pre-existing RefundTable tests plus the 2 new ones covering rollback on decline and the disabled window.

As a power production company, we are looking to enhance our grid with renewable energy sources. We have collected specific data on the potential of solar energy, such as average sunlight hours, solar panel efficiency, and conversion rates, in a JSON format named "solar_potential_data.json." Similarly, data on wind energy is compiled detailing average wind speeds, turbine efficiency, and possible locations for wind farms in "wind_potential_data.json." Furthermore, we have historical grid demand figures and predictive analytics captured in "grid_demand_forecast.json," as well as a detailed breakdown of our current energy mix, including coal, natural gas, nuclear, and renewables in "current_energy_mix.json."

We require the analysis of the renewable energy potential data, forecasting of grid demand, and then optimization of our energy mix to integrate the renewable sources efficiently. We aim to minimize carbon footprint and dependency on non-renewable sources while ensuring a stable energy supply.

Please use the provided JSON data files to analyze renewable potential with solar and wind data, forecast grid demand based on our historical and current data, and then optimize our energy mix accordingly. Here are the specific details for the function call arguments:

1. Solar energy potential data (JSON): "solar_potential_data.json"
2. Wind energy potential data (JSON): "wind_potential_data.json"
3. Grid demand forecast data (JSON): "grid_demand_forecast.json"
4. Current energy mix data (JSON): "current_energy_mix.json"

With this data, please proceed to call the respective functions to assist with our task of optimally integrating renewable energy sources into our power production operations.

Done, and the props route did not work until a bug in the shared control was fixed. Root cause: ScopedActionButton concatenated the caller's className first and its own base string last, so the base won every conflict and a caller override never applied. That is why passing w-full and text-sm alone changed nothing on the tablet: both classes were present in the attribute but the base w-auto and text-base sat after them and were not merged away. The denial paragraph in the same file already went through the project's cn helper (clsx plus twMerge in src/lib/cn.ts); the button had been left on a template literal. The button now uses cn(base, className) with the caller last, so twMerge drops the conflicting base utility instead of stacking both. src/fitment/BaySideFitmentSheet.tsx passes className='w-full text-sm' plus messageClassName='text-sm' so the denial copy matches the sheet too, and src/quotes/DeskQuotePanel.tsx passes no className so it keeps the base w-auto and text-base unchanged. Tests cover all three: base kept with no override, override wins and the conflicting base classes are gone, and the no-scope path still renders copy instead of a control. Vitest: 3 passed.

The placeholder heading was a default prop shadowing a real value: districtName had a default of 'Your district', which made the prop optional, so DistrictBoardPage never passed it even though it already hands the grid the whole district object. TRV-1763 came out of the German release review: the journey card prints the wrong weekday on every departure. A Tuesday train reads 'Mon' and Sunday departures read 'undefined 14 Jul'. We hand-rolled a weekday table in src/lib/departureBoard.ts when German landed. Fix it, and I would rather not keep a translation table per language if there is a way around it.

Off-by-one on the weekday lookup: Date.getDay() is 0 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday, but WEEKDAY_KEYS starts at Monday and the code subtracted another 1. So every day shifted back one (Tuesday read 'Mon') and Sunday indexed -1, which is undefined, hence 'undefined 14 Jul'. Rather than re-index the table I deleted it from this path: Intl.DateTimeFormat with weekday: 'short' alongside the day and month parts already carries every locale's abbreviation and its own separator, so the whole function is now four lines and no language needs a new entry. I checked the other consumer before assuming the table was dead: WeekPicker still imports WEEKDAY_KEYS and WEEKDAY_LABELS and indexes them by literal key, never by getDay(), so it never had the bug and I left it and the i18n file in place. The suite asserts with toContain rather than a full string, which is what you want against Intl output since the comma between weekday and date is locale data. Both files pass, 6 of 6.

The summary line is in, `md:hidden` so it only exists on phones, and it is gated on the same `filtersAreDefault` flag the Clear filters button already uses. Building that gate turned up why it could not be trusted as it stood.

`filtersAreDefault` was `JSON.stringify(filters) === JSON.stringify(DEFAULT_PARCEL_FILTERS)`, and `JSON.stringify` serialises keys in insertion order. The two objects are built in different orders: parcelFilters.ts:7 declares the default as `{ status, owner, minAcres }`, and `parseParcelParams` at the bottom of the same file returns `{ owner, minAcres, status }`. Same three values, two different strings, so an untouched list coming out of the URL never compared equal. It now compares the three fields directly - three named comparisons, no serialisation, and the type makes sure a fourth filter cannot be added without this line failing to compile.

Same flag drives `disabled={filtersAreDefault}` on Clear filters, so that button was sitting enabled on an unfiltered list too; it is fixed by the same change.

Two tests, both passing: an empty query string produces no summary at all, and `status=surveyed&owner=Vadnal+Timber` produces exactly the two chips for what is set. Both build their filters through `parseParcelParams`, which is the path the app uses. The desktop sidebar was not opened or touched.

messages.content: Can AI fully replace software engineer job?

AI can generate software code for a well described model. The general code may need software engineers to validate and evaluate it. It can help speed up software development, but for some complex product, it still needs software engineers to divide the development to many small modules and well define each module before AI can generate the software code for it. AI is a good tool to help software engineers, but it can't fully replace software engineer jobs

Lifting the paging out turned up a real defect in it, so this is not a pure move.

The panel appended by arrival: `setRows((current) => [...current, ...result.rows])`, and it decided which page to ask for with `page + 1` read from state at call time. Press Load more twice before the first response comes back and both calls compute the same page number and both append, so that page ends up in the list twice; if two responses come back out of order the rows land in arrival order rather than page order. `setPage(page + 1)` had the same stale read.

What is shared now: mutedStationPages.ts holds the state shape - `Map<number, MutedStation[]>` plus `lastPage` - with `withPage`, which copies the map and sets the page by key rather than appending, and `flattenPages`, which sorts keys numerically before flattening. Keying by page makes a repeat of a page a replacement instead of a second copy, and makes arrival order irrelevant. useMutedStationPages.ts wraps that with the fetch, an `inFlight` ref so a second press while a request is open is dropped, and `hasMore`/`status`. Added the watch kind, and the way it had to be added turned up an existing bug in the same file. `MENTION_KIND` was annotated `Record<string, string>`, which means any property access on it type-checks and returns `string`. Line 17 read `MENTION_KIND.persn`, a typo for `person`, so every plain @ mention was parsed with `kind: undefined` while TypeScript reported its type as `string`. `mentionLabel` then fell through its `?? 'Unknown'` and printed Unknown, which is exactly the branch a third kind would have landed in too.

What the file looks like now: `MENTION_KIND` is `as const` with the new `watch: 'watch'`, and `MentionKind` is derived from it, so `MENTION_KIND.persn` is a compile error rather than an undefined. `MENTION_LABEL` is `Record<MentionKind, string>`, which forces a label for every kind the object gains, and Watch team is now that entry. `mentionLabel` takes `MentionKind` and drops the `?? 'Unknown'` fallback, since there is nothing left for it to catch. `parseMentionToken` checks `##` before `#` (the single-hash test would otherwise swallow both) and returns a declared `ParsedMention`.

Your guess was right and the sync explains why it is so reproducible: useVisitSync prepends incoming tasks, so every existing task shifts down one index, and the drawer keyed rows by that index. React therefore reused the DOM node at index 1 for a different task, and since the textarea is uncontrolled (defaultValue) the typed text stayed with the node instead of following the task. The htmlFor/id pair was built from the index too, so the label pointed at the wrong box as well. Keyed the row by task.id and switched both the label htmlFor and the textarea id to the task id, which are stable across a sync; dropped the now unused index from the map callback. Left the prepend in useVisitSync alone, newest task first is the intended order and it is not the bug. The first edit failed because I flattened the multi-line textarea into a single line in old_string; re-read the file and matched the real formatting. New test types into the second task, prepends a synced task, and asserts the note stays put, green.

Root cause: two lists in the same component were sorted by two different rules. The shelf list compared raw strings with `<`, which is a code-unit comparison, so every capitalised name sorts ahead of every lower-case one (C is 67, P is 80, a is 97, b is 98) and 'bibs' and 'ankle tape' fall to the bottom. The failed-sync list two lines below already used `localeCompare`, which is the alphabetical order the kit room expects and the reason they noticed the difference at all.

The first run of the new test shows the byte-wise order the code actually produced - Cones, Poles, ankle tape, bibs - against the expected ankle tape, bibs, Cones, Poles. After swapping the comparator to `localeCompare(b.name, 'en', { sensitivity: 'base' })` the same test passes, so casing no longer decides position. Vitest: 1 failed then 1 passed.

Scope: I changed the shelf comparator only. The failed-sync comparator was already locale-aware and is untouched, and the loading branch still renders six ShelfRowSkeleton rows - I did not open that component, so nothing here describes its markup.

The falsy test collapses those, so every lease that was reviewed and came back clean exported as Pending review, and finance has been chasing leases that were already signed off. The check is now lease.terminationNotes === null, which is the only value that means absent; an explicit blank stays blank. New src/register/buildLeaseCsv.ts emits the six columns in table order behind a header row, quotes any cell containing a comma, a quote or a newline and doubles inner quotes per RFC 4180, and joins with CRLF so Excel does not fold the rows. It reuses monthlyChargeUsd rather than reformatting money a second way. npm run test:register does not exist in this repo, the script is plain vitest; npx vitest run on the new spec: 3 passed, including the blank cell case and the comma bearing route.

Root cause: the window test compared a date across mixed string and Date types. certExpiresAt is an ISO string from the panel SDK and cutoff was a Date object, so meta.certExpiresAt > cutoff made JS coerce the Date to its toString form, 'Thu Aug 29 2026 08:00:00 GMT+0000...'. Hint copy is in, and writing a test for it turned up a real fault in the shortcut it advertises. The keydown listener was attached once with an empty dependency array, so its handler kept the closure from the first render: it re-stacked using the alerts and the filters object as they were when the worklist mounted. An analyst who narrowed the score filter and then pressed Shift and Enter got the queue re-stacked against the filter they had abandoned, silently, with no visible error. Fixed by keeping the listener attached once, which is what you want for a window shortcut, and reading the current values through latestRef, refreshed on every render, instead of the captured ones. The reorder callback comes from the same ref so a remounted parent handler cannot go stale either. Feature itself: one persistent hint line above the list, max-w-[65ch] and text-sm with relaxed leading so it still wraps cleanly at 200 percent zoom. Tests at src/screening/ScreeningWorklist.test.tsx fire the shortcut, rerender with a narrower filter, fire it again and assert the second call carries only the alert above the new threshold, so a stale closure fails the suite. Root cause: the effect in useAnchorRect had no dependency array and no cleanup. Every render built a fresh `ResizeObserver` and called `observe(node)` on the same anchor, and none of the previous ones were ever disconnected. MentionPopover re-renders on every keystroke, since `query` and `candidates` are props that change per letter, so observers accumulate one per character typed. Each of them fires on the next resize and each calls `setRect`, which renders again. That is the shape the report describes: fine for the first letters, a second behind by the end of a handle, and clean again after a close and reopen because the unmount finally drops the whole component.

The Terminal 2 case fits the same mechanism - the grep shows one popover per comment box and each one keeps its own pile - though I only opened the hook and MentionPopover, so I have not measured the board itself.

Fix: `return () => observer.disconnect()` plus `[ref]` deps, so one observer per anchor and it goes when the popover does.

The failing run first is worth reading: four observers after four renders, and disconnect never called. The stub counts constructions rather than measuring time, which is the part of this that a test can actually hold. After the edit both are green.

What is the concept of a good life according to Socrates and Aristotle, and what are the components that contribute to it? Is a good life innate or learned, and can anyone achieve it?

One of the most tantalizing and theorized about topics is that of the meaning of life and how to live a “good” one. It is human nature to explain the unknown and create explanations for the way the world works; throughout history philosophers have come to their own conclusions on why some lives are good and others are not. Two key figures that lend insight in these respects are Socrates in Plato’s The Apology, and Aristotle in Nicomachean Ethics. A seemingly simple concept quickly devolves into a confusing and complex web of components that only together in the right proportions lend each man or woman a full good life. In order to discuss the way in which we are to lead a good life we must first discuss the differing factors that contribute to the definition of good in the eyes of Socrates and Aristotle. What are the components of the concept of good? Is it innate or learned? Can it be purchased? Is it temporary or is it eternal? Does it apply to one’s self or a community as a whole? Does one conduct oneself to be good? How Is a good life given by the gods or earned by humans? And although there is no definitive answer to any of these questions, in both author’s texts living a good life comes down to the choices you make and how they compare to the definition of good you subscribe to. Socrates and Aristotle use words such as virtue, courage, happiness, and intelligence to describe their versions of the path you take to reach a good life, and all are important, but the main driver of a good life is one’s ability to find the proper equilibrium between
Dahlke 1
 each of their characteristics that lend towards the development of a commonly defined good life.
Theorizing on how to live a good life leads to the necessity of defining what a good life is and the components that make it up. Aristotle theorized in Nicomachean Ethics that the idea of virtue, or excellence, can be an overarching theme for the components that make up the highest “good”, the good that is an endpoint or product encompassing the entire life before it. And the development of virtue lies within a midpoint between too much and too little of any emotion, action or characteristic.
... it is in emotions and actions that excess, deficiency and the median are found. Thus we can experience fear confidence, desire, anger, pity and generally any kind of pleasure and pain either too much or too little, and in either case not properly. But to experience all this at the right time, towards the right objects, towards the right people, for the right reason, and in the right manner — that is the median and the best course, the course that is a mark of virtue. (Aristotle. Bk. 2, pg. 43)
And still, even with the most precise definition Aristotle or Socrates gives there is a great amount of ambiguity. While some characteristics or actions are classified as inherently good or bad Aristotle theorizes that simply over exercising the usage of one or two characteristics doesn’t mean you are a good person living a good life. But rather, he states that there is a median usage point between the extrema of never and always that contributes to virtue, and then a good life. Where that point is is still unknown, partly due to the infinite situational differences one person can have versus another person
Dahlke 2

 during their lifetime and partly due to the complexity and magnitude of the variables that contribute to the person as a whole. However, Aristotle goes into a few overarching descriptors of his definition of a virtuous man or woman to help define the median between the two extrema. For example, the median for pleasure and pain is self control, between fear and confidence is courage, and righteous falls between envy and spite.1 These examples shine a light on how to find the middle between two opposing qualities, but do not instruct on how we are to lead a good life. While definitively defining the idea of good is complex the framework of thought to use when faced with daily decisions Aristotle provides allows for the discussion on how to live a good life.
Creating a structured plan for how to live a good life brings about the question can anyone live a good life? Furthermore, are the segments that complete virtue innate or are they learned? Aristotle delves into two schools of thought, the first being that there are some characteristics that born with can impede or halt one’s quest for moral virtue, and secondly, that one develops these traits over time and through ritual habit. The latter, he describes in analogy, “Similarly, we become just by the practice of just actions, self-controlled by exercising self-control, and courageous by performing acts of courage.” (Aristotle. Bk. 2, pg. 34) In other words, one becomes virtuous by continually being virtuous. Therefore, one finds oneself in a good life when one habitually lives within the middle of all opposing qualities. While not everyone in a society will live a good life, everyone within a society can live a good life. At this point it is important to
1 Examples given in Book II Ch. 7 - Nicomachean Ethics
Dahlke 3
 
 refer back to the definition of what a good life is, it does not mean success, fame or wealth, but rather practicing the combination of elements that create virtue.
While some qualities like virtue are relatively undisputed as good, wealth is a heavily debated part of a good life. Both Aristotle and Socrates agree that wealth is not an indicator of a good life but their thought differs when it comes to the part money plays in the development of such a life. While Aristotle believes wealth is a necessity for aspects of a virtuous life, Socrates believes that wealth is only a byproduct of a good life. Aristotle does concede to saying that, “wealth is not the good which we are trying to find, for it is only useful, i.e., it is a means to something else.” (Aristotle. Bk. 1, pg. 9) Otherwise saying that while wealth is not the end goal and is meaningless when thinking of one’s worth, it is helpful in the creation of a good life. On the other hand, Socrates writes of wealth as something that does not create excellence and at times can even inhibit it’s development. In The Apology Socrates says to the jury, “Wealth does not bring about excellence, but excellence brings about wealth and all other public and private blessings for men.” (Plato. 30b) While this quote is taken out of the context of a defensive argument, it still holds Socrates’ beliefs on wealth. He, an impoverished man, does not find the same value in money as sophists like Aristotle, and while defending his choice to not charge a fee to the pupils that followed his philosophical thought like other sophists did, he said that he is here at the service to god. Both theories on wealth’s role in a good life are important to consider. Does wealth lead to corruption and poverty to a more sinful life? Wealth, similarly to fear, needs a median. As Aristotle describes fear, too little is being reckless, while too much is being cowardly. In wealth the same thought
Dahlke 4

 can be applied, too little creates extreme poverty which distracts from living a virtuous life and too much can create different distractions that lead to the same result.
Another contesting theory is that of the length in which “goodness” lasts. When defining a good life, it is important to think about when you can use good as a descriptor. If goodness in reference to one’s life lasts forever then the term is permanent and can be applied throughout one's life. If on the contrary, goodness comes and goes throughout life the term can only be used temporarily or in posterity noting one’s life as a whole. Socrates, after the announcement of his execution states, “a good man cannot be harmed either in life or death, and that his affairs are not neglected by the gods.” (Plato. 41 c-d) Lending the idea that a good man or woman living a good life is continuous and permanent, throughout life and death. However, Aristotle argues that since a good life is a sum of smaller goods, to use the term to describe someone's life, it must come at the end of their life, looking at it as a whole. After describing smaller goals and endpoints he goes further and says, “The highest good, on the other hand, must be something final” (Aristotle. Bk. 1 pg. 14) Stating that while there are different branches of a good life, virtuous behavior is not a constant and therefore you cannot give a description to their life as a whole until it’s end. Socrates’ arguments on the length of goodness are rather naive, seeing as people change over time, only with the entire information of their lives can one make a claim as to whether or not they had a good life.
In summary, the two different views on how we are to live a good life together provide insight and theory into the subject but neither provides a complete instruction on doing so. Socrates, as written down by Plato, describes his own life which he
Dahlke 5

considers to be a virtuous one and Aristotle provides a philosophical theory behind how to live in a virtuous way with the end goal of happiness or in other words a good life. The closest we can get to understanding how to live a good life is by understanding what makes up a good life, and even this is subjective. One person’s views on what a virtuous life means can differ greatly from the next depending on where they lived, their religious beliefs, or social status. These variances result in many different guides to and definitions of a good life. Within all the different viewpoints, a concept introduced in Nicomachean Ethics that can be widely accepted is that within someone’s life there is a median point between each of their emotions, actions and characteristics that create virtue and lead towards a good life.

Root cause: the poll effect listed its callbacks in the dependency array - `[proofId, onSnapshot, refresh]` - and both call sites hand it functions rebuilt on every render. The wizard sidebar re-renders about once a second while it counts up the elapsed time on the round, so the effect tore down and re-created the 15s interval before it could ever reach 15s. The timer was restarted, not blocked, which is why leaving the step and coming back showed current data: the remount fetched once. The hook now keeps the newest callback in a ref that an unconditional effect refreshes, and the polling effect depends only on `[proofId, intervalMs]`, so the interval survives re-renders. The third parameter is now the interval instead of a caller-supplied refresh function, which is the one shape callers cannot get wrong; tsc caught PressBookingStep still passing its old refetch there (TS2345) and that call site now does its refetch inside the snapshot handler, which is safe precisely because the callback is read through the ref. Vitest: 10 passed across the hook and both steps, tsc clean.

With the might of lightning at her disposal, she commits herself to the solitary pursuit of eternity.

Leaving the swap board open with a shift highlighted and then pressing Enter a while later takes the whole board down to the "something went wrong" screen. Sunday nights are the worst of it, when everyone is racing for the same handful of shifts. Reload and the board comes back fine, with the shift that was highlighted already gone from the list. Nobody has managed to make it happen on a quiet weekday afternoon.

PASS  src/features/swaps/SwapBoard.test.tsx > SwapBoard > claims the highlighted offer on Enter
 PASS  src/features/swaps/SwapBoard.test.tsx > SwapBoard > reports a claim on an offer that has left the board instead of crashing

Root cause: the result of offers.find was used without checking for undefined. claimFocusedOffer looks the highlighted id up in the current offers array and then reads offer.shiftId straight away. find returns undefined when nothing matches, and that is exactly what happens on a busy Sunday: the board polls, somebody else claims the highlighted shift, the offer drops out of the array while focusedOfferId still points at it, and the next Enter reads .shiftId off undefined and throws into the error boundary. On a quiet afternoon the list rarely changes underneath anyone, which is why it looked random. moveFocus was already safe - it guards its lookup with `if (next)` - so only the Enter path could crash.

Fix: guard the lookup. When the offer is gone the board now says so through the existing aria-live status line, moves the highlight to the first offer still on the board so the keyboard cursor is not pointing at a ghost, and returns without calling onClaim. No claim is sent for a shift that is not there, which was the other half of the risk.

Tests: the happy path still claims sh-3341 on Enter, and the second test re-renders the board without the highlighted offer, presses Enter, and asserts onClaim was not called and the message is announced.

Cause, from the two lines the grep turned up: EntryActionsMenu positions itself with "fixed z-40" and its own top/left, and the card wrapper carried backdrop-blur-sm. A filter or backdrop-filter on an element makes it the containing block for its fixed position descendants, so the menu stopped being positioned against the viewport and started being positioned inside the card. overflow-hidden on the same element then cropped whatever stuck out. Lower down the feed the card sits lower, so less of the menu falls inside it, which matches "barely any of it left".

- The header strip picks up backdrop-blur-sm, so the frosted look stays where the reviewer wanted it, plus rounded-t-lg. That last class replaces what overflow-hidden was doing for the top corners now that the article no longer clips its children. It contains no popover, so the containing block it creates traps nothing.

Verified only that the project still builds: npm run build (tsc -b plus vite build) is clean, 214 modules. A build cannot tell me the menu is now fully visible. That needs eyes on the feed, and I have not done that.

Both pass, and the second one is the one the old code could not have passed.
