Root cause: the panel measures itself with a ResizeObserver and defers the measurement into `window.requestAnimationFrame`. The cleanup disconnected the observer but never cancelled the frame, so the last callback - the one fired by the panel collapsing to zero height as it is removed - still ran, computed `Math.max(1, Math.floor(0 / 40))` which is 1, and called `onRowsMeasured(1)` after the component was gone. The intake page keeps that number, which is why the next open offers a single time, and why a window resize clears it: that produces a fresh measurement. Escape misses it because that path does not shrink the panel first.

Fix: hold the frame id in the effect scope and cancel it alongside the disconnect. Five lines, no new imports, `useRef` and `useState` were already in use for the panel ref and the row count.

The test stubs ResizeObserver, since jsdom has none, and drives it by hand under fake timers. First case proves a 320px panel still reports 8 rows. Second emits a 0px measurement, unmounts, then advances past the frame and asserts the callback was called exactly once - it fails without the cancel because the queued frame reports again. Vitest: 2 passed. I did not open FnolIntakePage, so where the number is stored on that side is unverified here.

Found the afternoon slowdown before building the table. useComplianceStream called subscribeComplianceChecks inside its effect and returned nothing, so the socket was never closed: compliance.ts hands back a () => socket.close() teardown and the hook was throwing it away. Deps were already [shipmentId], which made it worse rather than better, every shipment a dispatcher opened left another live socket pushing into a dead setState, so 40 shipments a shift meant 40 open sockets and 40 React state updates per push. The effect now returns a cleanup that calls unsubscribe, so React closes the old socket on unmount and before re-running for a new shipment. The test is new alongside the fix and pins both halves: unsubscribe is not called while mounted, is called exactly once on unmount, and switching shipments tears the first stream down before the second is opened. DangerousGoodsTable itself is a plain semantic table keyed on unNumber with scope="col" headers and an sr-only caption, the outcome column spells out the state ('Blocked, cannot load' rather than a red dot) because nobody should read a DG hold off a colour, tabular-nums on UN numbers and class so the columns align, shipping name truncates with a title in a min-w-0 cell, an undeclared shipment gets a real empty message, and every colour ships its dark: pair. Vitest: 2 passed.

Root cause: the viewport effect had an early return in the middle of it. 'if (!live) return' fires after ro.observe(el) but before the cleanup function is returned, so every paused render created a ResizeObserver that was never disconnected. Toggle live a few times and a stack of live observers all keep calling setViewport, which is exactly the slow-then-slower scroll. The fix makes the listener registration conditional instead of the function exit, so one cleanup path always runs and disconnects the observer plus removes the scroll listener. SensorGrid.tsx is 2,318 lines and read_file truncated it, so I grepped for the useEffect line numbers and re-read only 1170-1201 to get the exact block. The render path is untouched, the scroll listener stays passive, and vitest is green: two new observer tests plus the existing rowWindow suite, 7 tests total.

Fixed in src/trade-in/hooks/useAppraisalSubmit.ts. Root cause: the validation bail-outs return out of submit and leave the progress bar at whatever value the last step set. The finalize-scope check sits after setProgress(60), so an appraiser without canFinalize gets an error message and a bar frozen at 60 for the rest of the session; the missing-VIN bail-out does the same thing at 35. The finally block was already there but only cleared the submitting flag, so the one piece of state that survived the bail-out was the bar. Now the same finally resets progress on every exit path, keeping 100 if the run actually reached the finalize step, so a knocked-back submit empties the bar and the next attempt starts from zero. Both bail-outs are covered by one reset rather than a setProgress(0) copy-pasted next to each return. Ran the suite with a glob first and vitest matched nothing, so the explicit test path was used instead. Vitest: 3 passed, including the case that the success path still ends at 100.

There is no useRunArchive.ts; the archive data layer is src/archive/runArchive.ts, found by grepping src/archive for nextCursor.

Building the warm ahead turned up something that had to be dealt with first. loadArchivePage fetched the runs and the column stats with Promise.all, so a rejected stats request threw away the runs that had already arrived. Warming the next page would have doubled the number of chances for that to happen, in the background, where nobody is watching. Promise.allSettled is what that pair actually wanted: the runs are the page, the stats are a garnish.

Change (src/archive/runArchive.ts, one edit):
- fetchArchivePage does the pair with Promise.allSettled, rethrows only if the runs request rejected, and passes stats: null when the stats request rejected. ArchivePage already declared stats as ColumnStats | null, so nothing downstream changes shape.
- A module level Map named warmed holds one promise per cursor. loadArchivePage takes a warmed page if it has one, then starts the page after the one it just returned. A first page load (cursor null) clears the map, since a new filter makes warmed cursors meaningless. A rejected warm removes itself from the map, and the catch keeps it from becoming an unhandled rejection.
- The list component needs no change, which is what the ticket asked for.

Verified with a new test file, three cases: stats service returns 503 and the page still comes back with its runs and stats null; the runs request returns 500 and loadArchivePage rejects with "Run page request failed with status 500"; and a two page walk where the first load makes 4 fetch calls (its own pair plus the warm ahead) and the second load makes none, returning run CH-20389. All three pass.

Not verified here: RunArchiveList.tsx. The grep showed it reads page.nextCursor and I left it alone, so the claim that it needs no change rests on the return type being unchanged, not on a run of that component.

Two-part race fix in useSpeciesSearch. Priya: the numbers on Kalmar Ridge right now are the 09:40 pull, except they are not, they flipped back to what was on screen before I went through the tunnel
Tomas: same thing on Fenwick yesterday. it settles on the new readings and then a few seconds later it swaps to older ones on its own
Priya: only ever after we come out of a dead zone. hitting sync again fixes it until the next dead zone
Tomas: can someone take this before Thursday, the install crew reads wind straight off the tablet

RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/kestrel-field

 PASS  src/features/sync/useSiteSnapshot.test.ts (3 tests) 312ms
   useSiteSnapshot > ignores a retry that lands after a newer request
   useSiteSnapshot > does not let a late retry rewrite the offline copy
   useSiteSnapshot > still shows the newest payload when nothing raced

      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Duration  1.62s

Root cause: the automatic retry resolved after the fresh request and overwrote it. Coming out of a dead zone, the first load fails and schedules a retry four seconds later. That retry goes out over a connection that is barely up, so it is slow. Meanwhile Priya taps sync, that request goes out on a good connection and lands first with the 09:40 readings. Seconds later the retry finally answers with what the edge had cached before the tunnel, and because nothing checked whether it was still the request anyone was waiting for, it called setSnapshot and writeCachedSnapshot with the older payload. That is the flip Priya and Tomas are describing, and it also poisoned the offline copy, which is why the stale numbers survived a reload until the next manual sync.

Fix: load stamps each attempt with an incrementing latestAttempt ref and bails out on both the success and the failure path if a newer attempt has started since. The last request to be issued is now the only one allowed to write state or the cache, regardless of which one answers first. Nothing else changed: the retry still fires, the cached copy still fills in while offline, and the error copy is unchanged. Tests cover the late retry losing to the manual refresh, the offline cache being written exactly once with the newest payload, and the ordinary uncontested load. Vitest: 3 passed.

Support forwarded this from a captain at Gatwick, their words, pasting it as it came in:

"Nine times out of ten the notes box on a fatigue report is simply not there. Blank panel with a Reload link where the box should be. If I have already written something on that report earlier in the day it comes back fine and I can carry on typing, it is the fresh ones that do it. Reloading does nothing at all. I have taken to writing them in the notes app on my phone and pasting them across, which is not ideal at 0600."

There is a second panel coming in the next sprint that wants the same drafts, so land the storage side of this as its own module rather than another copy inline.

RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/kestrel

 PASS  src/notes/noteDraft.test.ts (5 tests) 11ms
   readDraft > returns null for a report nobody has drafted on yet
   readDraft > returns null instead of throwing when the stored value is not JSON
   readDraft > returns null when the stored JSON is not a draft
   readDraft > gives back the draft that was written for that report
   readDraft > forgets the draft once it has been cleared

Root cause: the restore effect ran `JSON.parse(window.localStorage.getItem(draftKey(report.id)) as string)` and then read `stored.body`. On a report with no saved draft `getItem` returns null, `JSON.parse(null)` parses the string "null" and hands back null without throwing, so the throw came one line later on `stored.body` and took the whole panel down to the error boundary. That is why the captain sees it on fresh reports and not on ones already worked on: those have a key. The `as string` cast is what let it past strict mode in the first place.

Built src/notes/noteDraft.ts as asked: `readDraft` checks for a missing key, parses inside a try, and rejects anything that is not a `{ body, savedAt }` pair of strings, returning `NoteDraft | null` in every case; `writeDraft` and `clearDraft` own the key format so the next panel cannot spell it differently. CrewNoteThread now imports the three and falls back with `stored?.body ?? ''`, so an absent draft is an empty box rather than a crash.

Verified against the four ways it can go wrong, all five cases green: no key, non-JSON in the key, JSON that is not a draft, and the round trip plus clear. I did not open the second panel, it does not exist yet, and I have not tested CrewNoteThread's rendering here.

Added the save step, and it could not work until an existing fault was cleared. The effect that loads the agenda had an object literal in its dependency array: const query = { meetingId, section: 'agenda' } is rebuilt on every render, so [query] is a new reference every time, the effect re-ran on every render, each load called setItems with a fresh array and that render scheduled the next load. Any order the chair dragged was replaced by the next response a moment later, which is why a save button would have posted whatever the last fetch returned. Fixed by depending on the primitive that actually identifies the request, [meetingId], and building the query object inside the effect body where its identity does not matter. Then the feature: a Save order button that hands onSaveOrder the current item ids, disabled while the agenda is empty, with persistent copy beside it saying the order is not stored until pressed. Tests at src/board/minutes/AgendaBuilder.test.tsx assert loadAgendaItems is called exactly once for a meeting, and that an alt plus arrow reorder is what reaches onSaveOrder. Vitest: 2 passed.

Root cause: two writers, no coordination between them. Every keystroke armed a 600ms autosave through `scheduleAutosave`, and `handlePost` posted immediately without cancelling it. Post inside that 600ms window and the order on the wire is `status: 'posted'` first, then the autosave firing with the body as it was at the last keystroke and `status: 'draft'` - the later write wins on the server, so the stored note is the older text. The failing run shows exactly that pair, posted then draft, both for the same flight key. The note reads correctly for a moment because the optimistic thread entry comes from `onPosted(draft)` before the autosave lands.

Fix, both in RebookingNoteDock.tsx: `cancelAutosave()` runs at the top of `handlePost`, so an armed timer never fires after a post; and a `postingRef` closes the narrower window where the timer has already fired and the request is in flight, since a ref is readable from inside the timeout without re-arming it. `postingRef` is cleared in the same `finally` that clears the posting state, so a later edit still autosaves normally.

The middle test is there to keep the fix from being a sledgehammer: an untouched note still saves its draft after 600ms. The third one covers what the desk sees, the parent gets the full body and the box empties.

Scope: I read RebookingNoteDock.tsx in full and only line 806 of DisruptionDeskPage.tsx, which is where the dock is rendered. Whether anything else on that page writes to the same note record I have not checked.

Why is crypto currency risky?

Cryptocurrency is risk for a number of reasons.  The price fluctuations are usually driven by large institutional investors not individuals.  When institutions pull out their money you can see price fluctuations as high as 90% loss.  It is a deregulated digital currency with no government oversight so if your money gets hacked or taken because a bad actor got your wallet keys your money is lost for good, you will never get it back, and there will never be an investigation into where your money went.  If you are going to play in the crypto currency space its best to use a platform similar to coinbase that has security measures in place for all your crypto wallets so your money doesn't get stolen.

Extract names of all weapons mentioned in the paragraph below:

In the late 18th century, French General Jean-Baptiste Vaquette de Gribeauval promoted standardized weapons in what became known as the Système Gribeauval after it was issued as a royal order in 1765. (Its focus at the time was artillery more than muskets or handguns.) One of the accomplishments of the system was that solid cast cannons were bored to precise tolerances, which allowed the walls to be thinner than cannons poured with hollow cores. However, because cores were often off center, the wall thickness determined the size of the bore. Standardized boring allowed cannons to be shorter without sacrificing accuracy and range because of the tighter fit of the shells. It also allowed standardization of the shells.
The following are names of weapons in the paragraph above: artillery, muskets, handguns, cannons, shells

The literal navigate('/queue string was not in the tree because the path is built from a template literal, so I searched for useNavigate instead and it pointed straight at ReviewForm.tsx. The double file was a pending flag that was set but never used: no disabled attribute, no early return, so the second click ran the whole handler again. The new action reuses the same handler with an openNext flag rather than a second copy of the submit path, and it is disabled when nextSubmissionId is null so the last review in a queue cannot navigate nowhere. Two halves of one race. The effect fires a fetch per region and calls setState unconditionally when it resolves, so a slow Frankfurt response landing after the switch overwrote the newer series; that is the wrong-region data ops saw. The same setState({ series: body }) also threw away any socket samples that had already arrived for the new region, which explains the missing live points. The effect now closes over a cancelled flag that its own cleanup sets, so a stale response is dropped instead of applied, and it keeps a local live array of samples the socket delivered while the snapshot was in flight, merged in on resolve. Merging is real work (dedupe by timestamp, sort ascending), so it went into its own module with a doc comment. I first wrote that helper to src/utils/, a directory tsconfig does not list in include and no path alias points at, so it would have compiled nowhere; reading tsconfig.json to pick the right alias caught it, the file now sits in src/lib behind @lib/*, and the stray copy is deleted. Two tests, one per half of the race, both green.

`useImperativeHandle` was built with an empty dependency array, so the object holding `jumpToNextUnweighed` was created once at mount and the `tickets.find(...)` inside it kept reading the array from that first render forever. Every refresh after that, the method was still hunting through the mount-time list, which is why it lands on a ticket that has since been weighed - and why it looks more wrong the longer the screen stays open. Adding `tickets` to the deps rebuilds the handle whenever the list changes; the toolbar reads it through a ref at call time (ScaleToolbar.tsx:24 in the grep), so nothing on that side needs changing.

Second note: the rows carry `tabIndex={-1}` and were being focused programmatically, but a JS `focus()` call does not satisfy `:focus-visible`, so a `focus-visible:` ring would have stayed invisible on exactly this path. The rows now use plain `focus:ring-2 focus:ring-amber-700 focus:ring-offset-2` with a lighter ring in dark mode, which does paint for a programmatic focus.

Two tests, both passing. The first mounts with one unweighed ticket, re-renders with a refreshed list where a different ticket is the unweighed one, then calls the handle and asserts focus is on the Nass Valley Chip row - that test fails on the old empty deps. The second checks the early return leaves focus on the body when nothing is unweighed. `scrollIntoView` is stubbed because jsdom does not implement it. I have not seen the ring on a real screen, only the class list; the focus behaviour itself is what the tests cover.

Root cause: saveRegistryOrder returns a promise and both reorder paths called it un-awaited, so setToast('Registry saved') ran on the same tick as the click. The green toast was reporting the local setOrder, never the write. A slow PATCH meant the owner closed the tab before it landed, and a rejected one still showed success, which is the three-attempts story in her email. Refactor: one applyOrder(pendingKey, next, doneMessage) owns both paths, awaits the save, and only then calls notifyToast('success', ...) from src/shared/notify. A rejection rolls setOrder back to the previous array and raises an error toast that names the problem and the retry. Both hand-built toast blocks and the local toast state are gone. While a save is in flight the row reads 'Saving' and every reorder control carries the real disabled attribute plus disabled:opacity-50 disabled:pointer-events-none, so a double write cannot happen. Conventions: gap-2 inside the list and gap-6 between blocks, min-h-11 targets, item names truncate with a title inside a min-w-0 cell, one rose accent, dark: variant on every colour, one shared rowActionClass so hover, focus-visible, active and disabled ship together, motion-reduce on the transitions. Vitest: 2 passed, the first asserts there is no toast before the promise settles.

Root cause: `endDrag` bailed out before it cleaned up. The guard `if (commentId === null || defectId === null) return` sat above the three lines that reset the drag - `draggingId.current = null`, `setIsDragging(false)` and `document.body.classList.remove(DRAG_CLASS)` - so a drag that ended anywhere except on a defect line left `dragging-pin` on `<body>` for the rest of the session. A drag that lands runs past the guard and cleans up, which is exactly the split Priya and Ola describe.

Fix: the reset runs first, unconditionally, and the guard now only decides whether `onAnchor` is called. Same lines, reordered, no new state.

Three cases pinned by the test: the dropped drag takes the class off and does not call `onAnchor`, the landed drag calls it once with the right pair, and a dropped drag followed by a real one still anchors the second comment. I have not opened the stylesheet that defines `.dragging-pin`, so I am not describing what it does beyond the class name; the test asserts the class comes off the body, not the cursor or selection behaviour on the page.

Root cause: the copy was one level deep. `cloneWeekPlan` spread the plan and mapped `plan.days` into fresh day objects, which is why the copy could get its own id and its own start date and looked like a real copy. Moving the Tuesday visit to 11:00 wrote into the object both weeks were holding, which is why the original moved too and why the printed schedule agreed with the screen. Fixed by mapping the visits as well, `visits: day.visits.map((visit) => ({ ...visit }))`, so each level the caller can edit gets a new object.

They are the same bug. The effect depends on pathname, so it re-ran on every navigation, but it never returned a cleanup - so each route change added another keydown listener on window while the old ones stayed alive. After n navigations one chord fired n navigate calls, which is exactly the doubled history entry Marta saw. The effect now returns removeEventListener for the exact handler it registered, and navigate joins the dependency array since the handler closes over it. Adding collections was then a one-line entry in JUMP_TARGETS - the handler is table-driven, so no new branch. SkipLink was the other addEventListener hit but it registers with { once: true } on a node it owns, so it is fine. New test covers all three behaviours: the chord navigates, the old listener is removed on route change (this is the regression, it would have been 0 removals before), and nothing fires after unmount. parseChord's existing suite still passes untouched.

In our robotics lab, we are currently upgrading the precision of our RM-2045 robotic manipulator. We have equipped it with an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensor and plan to employ the Factored Quaternion Algorithm combined with a Kalman Filter for enhanced orientation estimates. The objective is to ensure the orientation accuracy of this manipulator is within stringent tolerances for our upcoming high-precision tasks.

Separately, given the identified orientation data, we aim to refine the manipulator's operation by estimating its kinematic parameter errors using an Extended Kalman Filter. This process is essential for correcting any deviations that might impede the robot's performance across its range of motion.

To proceed with these calibration steps, I request the execution of function calls to estimate both the orientation of the robotic manipulator RM-2045 using the FQA_KF algorithm with the IMU sensor, and subsequently to estimate the kinematic parameter errors based on the acquired orientation estimation data using the EKF algorithm. These actions are critical for our laboratory's capability to perform high-precision robotic tasks.

Conservators are losing typing on the condition wizard. Carry on writing in the damage notes while the step is saving and about a second later the box snaps back to what it held when you pressed the button - anything typed in between is gone. Rhiannon lost most of a spine description that way this morning and has stopped trusting the step, she now types into a text file first and pastes it in afterwards.

It is not every time. It is only if you keep typing after you press save, which conservators do constantly because they are looking at the object, not at the screen.

That step is also the last one still hand-rolling its own promise chain, so bring it in line with the others while you are in it.

Root cause: `saveAndScore` took `const submitted = survey` before the await, then in the `.then` after that await wrote the captured object straight back with `setSurvey({ ...submitted, score })`. Everything typed while the save was in flight lived in the newer state, and the score callback replaced it with the pre-await snapshot, which is why it only bites people who keep typing after pressing save. The score now comes from an awaited call in the same try block, and the write is a functional update, `setSurvey((current) => ({ ...current, score }))`, so it merges into whatever the conservator has since typed instead of resurrecting an old copy. Dropping the mixed await-plus-`.then` also means a failing score fetch lands in the existing catch and the error message rather than going unhandled, and the step reads like the other steps in this wizard. The survey is never cleared on failure either, which the second test pins. Vitest: 2 passed.

AUD-1341 - Fieldbook waveform previews. Scroll the clip library for a couple of minutes and the tab pins a core at 100% and the fans come up. It is far worse on a folder that still has clips being analysed (peaks not back yet). My guess is we never stop the draw loop for those. src/library/WaveformPreview.tsx, the effect at the top of the component.

RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/fieldbook

 PASS  src/library/WaveformPreview.test.tsx (2 tests) 66ms
   WaveformPreview > disconnects the observer on unmount while the clip is still being analysed
   WaveformPreview > disconnects the observer on unmount for an analysed clip

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)

The killer was the `if (peaks.values.length === 0) return` sitting between observer.observe(canvas) and the cleanup: for any clip still being analysed the effect registered an observer and then bailed before returning a teardown, so that observer outlived the component, and its callback called drawFrame directly - a loop with no cancel handle attached to a canvas that had been unmounted. Scroll a folder of unanalysed clips and you accumulate one immortal rAF loop per row. Restructured so there is exactly one exit path with cleanup: the emptiness check moved inside the observer callback, the cleanup always cancels the frame and disconnects the observer. The loop also never terminated once the fill-in reached full height - it now stops at progress === 1 instead of re-scheduling forever, which is the rest of the CPU. Reduced motion draws the final frame in one pass rather than a slower ramp. My first pass typechecked as TS2345 because dropping the null guard left observe() taking HTMLCanvasElement | null; the follow-up puts the guard back at the very top, before anything is registered, which is the one place an early return is safe here. Two new tests cover unmount teardown for both the empty and analysed cases; tsc is clean.

The li built its class list by string concatenation, so when the rules list passes className="bg-white dark:bg-zinc-950" the element ends up carrying both bg-white and bg-amber-50. Two utilities of the same property in one class attribute are not resolved by their order in the string, they are resolved by their order in the compiled stylesheet, so the pending tint lost every time in the app while storybook, which renders the row with no className at all, showed it fine. The row now merges through cn (clsx plus twMerge from src/lib/cn.ts, already used by the multiplier buttons in this same file), which drops the losing duplicate outright, and the pending class is passed last so it deliberately beats anything the parent sends. Also stopped signalling pending by colour alone: the secondary line now reads "Saving the new multiplier" while the request is in flight, which is what a screen reader and a colour-blind user get. Added the missing dark: pairs on the border and the pending tint. npx tsc --noEmit is clean.

Root cause: the fade's `onfinish` sets state after the element has left the tree. The effect starts a 200ms opacity animation on the skeleton list and hands it a finish handler that calls `setSkeletonVisible(false)`, but the effect returns nothing, so unmounting the board or changing squad mid-load leaves the animation running on a detached node. It finishes 200ms later and writes into a component that is gone, which is the act() noise Nadia sees, and when the same instance has already put a new squad's skeleton up it hides that one, which is Rob's blink.

Fix: return a cleanup that calls `fade.cancel()`. A cancelled animation fires cancel, not finish, so the stale handler cannot run at all - no unmounted check or ref flag needed.

Verified by test: the new spec stubs `Element.prototype.animate` with a recording double, drives the board from loading to loaded so one animation is created, then unmounts. Before the edit the run shows `expected false to be true` on the cancelled flag; after it, the same spec passes and `onfinish` is null. Vitest: 1 failed then 1 passed.

Scope note: the first read came back truncated (26 of 1240 lines), so I only ever saw the head and lines 287-337 that the grep pointed at. Everything outside that window is unread and unchanged, and PlayerAvailabilityRow was not opened, so nothing here describes the loaded row markup.

Root cause: downloadOutageReport created the object URL on its first line and only revoked it on the happy path at the bottom. Our company's network has recorded an unusual pattern of traffic distribution which could indicate a breach of security or system inefficiency. To address this, we've proactively captured raw network packet data over a period, which includes comprehensive details of inbound and outbound traffic. The data is saved in a JSON file named "network_traffic_data.json", which contains metadata such as timestamps, source and destination IPs, protocol information, and payload sizes for the past week.

We desire a deep analysis of this network packet data to detect any anomalies that might be causing the slowdowns or potential security threats. Notably, we're interested in finding discrepancies such as uncharacteristic bandwidth usage, connections from unrecognized IP addresses, or suspicious activities during off-peak hours.

To proceed with this analysis, I request the extraction of relevant traffic features from the "network_traffic_data.json" file, followed by detection of any anomalies within these features. After detecting the anomalies, a comprehensive summary report outlining the findings will be indispensable for our IT team to take appropriate action.

Here's the specific user query:

"Please utilize the 'extract_traffic_features' function to analyze 'network_traffic_data.json' and extract pertinent features such as IP addresses, protocols, timestamps, and payload sizes. Following this, leverage the 'detect_anomalies' tool to identify any abnormal patterns present in the extracted features. Finally, with the 'summarize_findings' function, create a detailed report based on the anomaly detection results for our IT team's review.” 

The "network_traffic_data.json" includes actual packet capture details and is structured as follows:
```json
{
  "packets": [
    {
      "timestamp": "1650582480.123456",
      "src_ip": "192.168.0.5",
      "dst_ip": "93.184.216.34",
      "protocol": "HTTPS",
      "length": "1500"
    },
    {
      "timestamp": "1650582490.654321",

      "dst_ip": "198.51.100.14",
      "protocol": "FTP",
      "length": "800"
    },
    // More packet entries...
  ]
}
```

This file represents a snapshot of the network traffic which we need to analyze for any irregularities.

The extraction of relevant traffic features from the "network_traffic_data.json" file has been completed. The features include timestamps, source and destination IP addresses, protocols, payload sizes, source and destination ports, and TCP flags. 

Here's a brief look at two of the extracted features:

1. A packet with the following details:
   - **Timestamp**: 1650582480.123456

   - **Destination IP**: 93.184.216.34
   - **Protocol**: HTTPS

2. Another packet with the details:

With the extracted features now available, the next step is to detect any anomalies within these features. To proceed, I will use the 'detect_anomalies' tool.

messages.content: What are the steps to care for a houseplant?

First, be sure to provide water, sunlight and humidity levels necessary for the variety of plant you have. For example, succulent-type plants may require less frequent waterings than their green-leafy counterparts. Research your new plants' preferred sunlight, water, and humidity requirements so you can provide the best care. Second, be sure to review your newly acquired houseplant for any pests before introducing them into your home. You’ll want to check the leaves for mealy bugs, spider mites, etc. and the soil for pests such as fungus gnats. If you find any of these be sure to quarantine your new plant away from your current plants and treat with a pesticide of your choosing. Many houseplant owners use neem oil to treat pests. Third, upsize or repot your plant only when it is ready. Your new plant likely will be happy for a while in its current nursery (plastic) container that it came home from the shop in. You can choose to upsize the pot once you notice signs of the plant being root bound (the roots take up a majority of the pot) such as water draining from the pot quickly and the soil not becoming saturated or the plant slows its growth of new leaves (unless its the winter season at which time plants naturally slow or stop new growth). Spring time is the best time to repot your plants.

messages.content: What is engineering culture?

Engineering culture often refers to common beliefs and behaviors of engineers within a company. A strong engineering culture allows engineers to work more effectively together.

Different engineers often have different understanding or beliefs on the same topic, such as whether a PRD is needed for a design doc, or whether an engineer should write tests for their work. Without a strong engineering culture, engineers often waste timing debating on nuances, which can significantly hurt business productivity and create poor customer experience.

Large technology companies often have strong and unique engineering culture. For example: Apple favors design and quality; Amazon favors customer experience; Facebook favors success metrics; Google favors engineering excellence; Microsoft favors business success. Each engineering culture has its pros and cons. In general, having an engineering culture is better than not having one. A good leadership should intentionally foster a strong engineering culture in their company.

Root cause: `retry` had nothing stopping a second call while the first was still open. Each tap set status to 'saving' and immediately awaited another `save(prefs)`, so three taps meant three requests in flight against the same record. `status` cannot act as the guard either - it is state, so the taps in one burst all read 'idle' before React re-renders. Whichever request the server finished last is the one that stuck, which is why the entry that survives is not always the last one tapped.

`useRetrySave` now holds an `inFlight` ref, set synchronously before the await and cleared in a `finally`, so a tap during a save is dropped and a tap after one is honoured whether it succeeded or failed.

I applied it to the wrong copy first. There are two files called retrySave.ts, one under settings/sync and one under settings/notifications, and I wrote the sync one. The two files were byte for byte identical - same missing guard - so both now carry it, and that duplication is the next thing to remove; I did not merge them here because the two panels pass different save functions and I have not opened either panel.

As the Operations Manager for a mid-sized apparel retailer, my objective is to refine our supply chain to address key operational inefficiencies. We have compiled extensive historical sales data over the past two years in a CSV format, which we would like to use to forecast inventory needs for the upcoming quarter of the year. Furthermore, we've tracked our supplier interaction over the same period, noting down key performance indicators in a separate CSV file to assess their delivery time, cost, and quality of goods. Lastly, we have detailed information on our current logistics operations and the geographical locations of our retail outlets compiled in a JSON format.

In order to advance our supply chain operations effectively, I request the use of functions to: 1) forecast our inventory needs for the next quarter by analyzing the provided historical sales data, 2) evaluate the performance of our suppliers using the metrics we have gathered to improve collaboration, and 3) optimize our distribution logistics to enhance the efficiency of deliveries to retail outlets. Below, you can find the details and actual data that should be passed into the function parameters.

1. Forecast inventory needs:
   - Historical Sales Data for the past two years (included as a JSON file):
     ```json
     {
       "sales": [
         { "date": "2021-01-01", "product_id": "A01", "units_sold": 150 },
         { "date": "2021-01-01", "product_id": "A02", "units_sold": 200 },
         ...
         { "date": "2022-12-31", "product_id": "A01", "units_sold": 180 },
         { "date": "2022-12-31", "product_id": "A02", "units_sold": 220 }
       ]
     }
     ```
   - Forecast Period: '2023-Q2'

2. Evaluate supplier performance:
   - Supplier Performance Metrics (included as a JSON file):
     ```json
     {
       "suppliers": [
         { "supplier_id": "S001", "delivery_time_days": 5, "quality_rate": 95, "cost": 1000 },
         { "supplier_id": "S002", "delivery_time_days": 6, "quality_rate": 90, "cost": 900 },
         ...
       ]
     }
     ```

3. Optimize distribution logistics:
   - Current Distribution Logistics Information (included as a JSON file):
     ```json
     {
       "logistics": [
         { "shipment_id": "L001", "outlet_id": "R001", "delivery_time_days": 2 },
         { "shipment_id": "L002", "outlet_id": "R002", "delivery_time_days": 3 },
         ...
       ]
     }
     ```
   - Retail Outlet Locations (included as a JSON file):
     ```json
     {
       "outlets": [
         { "outlet_id": "R001", "location": "New York, NY" },
         { "outlet_id": "R002", "location": "San Francisco, CA" },
         ...
       ]
     }
     ```

I would like to request the execution of functions utilizing the above-provided data to deliver insights that will help us streamline supply chain operations effectively.

1. **Forecast Inventory Needs**:

   - Product A02 is expected to need 120 units, considering a consistent demand for this product in Q2 with a slight upward trend.

2. **Evaluate Supplier Performance**:
   - Supplier S001 has a score of 90 and is praised for meeting delivery timelines with a high-quality rate, despite higher costs compared to industry standards.
   - Supplier S002 has a score of 85, offering slightly slower delivery and a lower quality rate, but is more cost-effective.
   - The evaluation considers average delivery time, quality rate, and cost data from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2022.

3. **Optimize Distribution Logistics**:
   - For shipment L001 to outlet R001 in New York, NY, it's recommended to consolidate shipments to reduce delivery times from 2 days to 1 day.

   - The recommendations focus on reducing delivery times and improving the efficiency of distribution to retail outlets, based on the current logistics data period from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2022.

Root cause: the transaction was opened before the date was checked, and the rejection branch returned straight out of the function. `const tx = await openScheduleTransaction(...)` on line one, then `if (problem) return { ok: false, problem }` with no commit and no abort, so the handle for that matter was left open and abandoned. Every later save went through that same line and stopped there, which matches the report exactly: no error text, the button appears dead, and a reload clears it.

Fix: the validation runs first, so a rejected date never opens anything, and the write path is wrapped in try/catch so a failed put aborts the handle instead of leaking it the same way. Two exits, both closing what they opened.

Vitest: 3 passed. One asserts the rejected date leaves openScheduleTransaction uncalled, one does a rejected save then a good one and checks the good one commits, one makes the put reject and checks abort is called once. validateHearingWindow is the real module, not a mock - the 12-04 draft falls outside the 11-02 to 11-30 window it compares against.

I did not open scheduleStore.ts, so why a second open never resolves once one is left dangling is unverified here. What is verified is that neither exit path leaves one behind now.

advance was wrapped in useCallback with an empty dependency array, so it closed over the queue from the first render forever. Click one worked, then every later click read that same stale array, called the same resident and set the queue back to the original tail. The queue therefore never reached zero and the empty panel could never render. The lazy fix is to stop memoising: advance is a plain function now, re-created each render, so it always sees current state, and nothing downstream is memoised to care. The existing suite passed because its click test only clicks once, which is exactly why the bug survived. npm run lint then failed, useCallback was left imported and unused, so I dropped it from the import and lint is clean. New empty state gives the clerk real copy plus a link to the sign-up sheet, and the Call next speaker button is now genuinely disabled with the disabled attribute when the queue is empty rather than sitting there live over an empty list.

Root cause: a forgotten await inside the save loop destroyed the ordering guarantee. putPreference is async, the for loop called it without await, so all three writes left the handset at once and the order they arrived in was down to whatever the site radio did that morning. The preferences endpoint is a read modify write on one document per guard, so the last request to land wins the whole document, and a request built from a snapshot taken before the theme write simply erased it. That is the whole shape of the report: sometimes the theme survives, sometimes only the text size, sometimes a density nobody chose, and never an error, because the local state was correct the entire time and only the stored document was wrong. Two side effects of the same missing await went away with it: the catch could never fire, since a rejected promise from an un-awaited call is not caught by the surrounding try, and setSaving(false) in the finally ran before a single write had landed, so the Saved label was a lie. Started at src/features/appearance/index.ts, which is an empty barrel, so I located the real hook by searching for putPreference callers instead of guessing at contents. New test drives the three writes through a mock whose latency is deliberately reverse ordered, 30ms then 10ms then 1ms, and asserts the completion order: 1 passed.

import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react'
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event'
import { afterEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest'

import * as api from '../../api/grading'
import { lineCScans } from '../../test/fixtures/gradeScans'
import { ScanFeed } from './ScanFeed'

afterEach(() => {
  vi.restoreAllMocks()
})

describe('ScanFeed flush', () => {
  it('keeps the buffered scans and reports the failure when the batch POST rejects', async () => {
    const persist = vi
      .spyOn(api, 'persistBatch')
      .mockRejectedValue(new Error('POST /api/grading/batches failed with 503'))
    render(<ScanFeed scans={lineCScans} lineId="C" />)

    await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send buffered scans' }))

    await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('still queued'))
    expect(persist).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
    expect(screen.getByText('12 scans buffered')).toBeInTheDocument()
  })

  it('clears the buffer once the batch is accepted', async () => {
    vi.spyOn(api, 'persistBatch').mockResolvedValue({ batchId: 'B-20260714-0031', accepted: 12 })
    render(<ScanFeed scans={lineCScans} lineId="C" />)

    await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send buffered scans' }))

    await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('0 scans buffered')).toBeInTheDocument())
    expect(screen.queryByRole('alert')).toBeNull()
  })
})

flushBuffer was async but called persistBatch without awaiting it, so the three lines that clear the buffer ran immediately while the POST was still in flight. On a 503 the promise rejected with nobody attached, which is the node unhandled rejection in the replay and, in the browser, a counter reset for scans that were never persisted. Awaiting inside try/catch/finally makes the clear conditional on success, surfaces a real message in the existing role=alert banner naming the count and telling the operator the scans are still queued, and keeps the pending flag correct on both paths. The two call sites can stay as bare flushBuffer() calls now that the function no longer rejects. ScanFeed.tsx is 2,905 lines and read_file returned nothing at all, so grep on the flush symbols gave me the line numbers and I read only 1466-1480. Both new tests pass, including the one that proves the buffer survives a failed batch.

Root cause: the team box was wired twice. The `<label>` wrapped the checkbox and carried its own `onClick={() => toggleWatcher(team.id)}`, while the `<input>` inside it also called `toggleWatcher` from `onChange`. A click anywhere in that label activates the checkbox and bubbles through the label, so both handlers ran and the second toggle undid the first - the box came back unticked and `watcherIds` stayed empty, which is exactly what the first run showed: `watcherIds: []` reaching `onSend` with the body intact. The intermittent pass QA saw is the same thing with a stray double click landing an odd number of toggles.

Fix: the wrapping label is now a plain `<div>`, the input gets `id={`watcher-${team.id}`}` and the name is a real `<label htmlFor=...>` next to it. One handler, `onChange`, stays. The accessible name is unchanged, which is why the test still finds the box with `getByLabelText('Ground power')` both before and after.

`handleSubmit` needed nothing: the failing run proved it already forwarded `turnaroundId`, the trimmed body and `watcherIds` in one object. I only opened ThreadComposer.tsx, so I cannot say whether other checkboxes in the app carry the same double wiring - worth a sweep, not checked here. Vitest: 2 passed.

RTL-2377: at the till a lead reloads a gift card and then sits in the dialog waiting for the receipt number before they can serve the next person in the queue. Make the confirmation come through as a toast carrying the receipt number, so the dialog takes itself off the screen and the queue keeps moving. The amount keypad stays exactly as it is, nobody wants that retrained.

RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/till-console

 PASS  src/tills/ReloadGiftCardDialog.test.tsx (2 tests) 288ms
   ReloadGiftCardDialog > toasts the receipt and only then closes the dialog

The ask was the toast, but the reason nobody got a receipt number in the first place is a real bug in the old handler: it called onClose() before the await and then kept going. onClose unmounts the dialog, so the await in the submit handler resumed on a component that was already gone, and setReceiptId and setSubmitting were writing state into a dead tree. The receipt paragraph could never render, React logged the update-on-unmounted warning at every till, and the toast that fired afterwards said only 'Gift card reloaded' because the receipt id was on the state that went nowhere. Fix: the handler awaits reloadGiftCard first, raises the toast through the shared notify bus, which is mounted on the app shell and therefore outlives the dialog, and calls onClose() last. Nothing is written to component state after that call, so there is no resume-after-unmount path left. A rejection is the only branch that touches state, and the dialog is still mounted there: submitting goes false, an error message names what happened and that nothing was charged, and the typed amount is preserved rather than cleared. Feature side: the toast carries the formatted amount, the last four digits and the receipt id, so the lead reads it and moves on. Cause: ExcursionPage declared status as optional while rows was declared required. Root cause: the effect cleanup detached both listeners but never closed the EventSource, so the connection was left open on unmount. A detached listener does not end the stream: the browser keeps the socket, and when the server ends its turn the EventSource reconnects on its own, which is the flood of reconnects from their office. Every trip into a request and back out again added another live stream, so a status change arrived once per surviving stream - the double live updates Naomi describes - and the pile of open connections is what made the board sluggish enough for a drag to be dropped. Fixed by calling source.close() in the cleanup, alongside the listener removal that was already there, and resetting connected to false so the live indicator is honest about a torn-down stream. Tests at src/features/dsar/useRequestStream.test.ts assert the stream is closed on unmount, and that switching case ids closes the old stream before opening the new one, so a cleanup that only removes listeners fails again. Vitest: 2 passed.

export interface MeterReading {
  serial: string
  siteName: string
  readAt: string
  kwh: number | null
  variance: number
}

export type ExceptionKind = 'no-read' | 'zero-consumption' | 'high-variance' | 'none'

const VARIANCE_LIMIT = 0.35

/**
 * Sorts one meter read into the exceptions queue. A dead panel returns a true
 * 0 kWh and needs a site visit; a meter we never heard from needs a comms check.
 */
export function classifyReading(reading: MeterReading): ExceptionKind {
  const kwh = reading.kwh || null
  if (kwh === null) return 'no-read'
  if (kwh === 0) return 'zero-consumption'
  if (reading.variance > VARIANCE_LIMIT) return 'high-variance'
  return 'none'
}

Repro
1. Sign in on an account that has only ever saved X band and Ku band settings
2. Open Preferences > Downlink
3. Click the Ka band tab

Expected: the Ka tab shows the account defaults and the summary line under the controls reads normally.
Actual: the panel area goes blank and the console reports a TypeError. Clicking back to X band brings it all back.

The same lookup is written out three times in that panel. Fold it into one accessor while you are in there, so the next band we add does not repeat it.

Root cause: `savedPrefs` is a `Map<BandId, BandPrefs>` and the panel read it three times as `savedPrefs.get(bandId) as BandPrefs`. The cast is the whole bug. `Map.get` returns `BandPrefs | undefined`, and for a band the account has never saved it returns undefined, which the cast then hands to `formatDownlinkSummary(prefs)` and to `prefs.polarisation` as though it were an object. X and Ku had saved entries, Ka did not, so only the Ka tab threw.

There is one accessor now. `resolveBandPrefs` returns `savedPrefs.get(bandId) ?? ACCOUNT_DEFAULT_BAND_PREFS[bandId]`, and the grep result shows `ACCOUNT_DEFAULT_BAND_PREFS` is declared in bandPrefs.ts as `Record<BandId, BandPrefs>`, so indexing it with the tab id yields a real object and the accessor's return type is `BandPrefs` with no cast left anywhere in the file. The three call sites became one call plus `prefs.symbolRateMbaud`, and the summary memo now depends on `prefs` rather than on the whole map.

Verified with `npx tsc --noEmit`, which is clean. That is a typecheck and nothing more: I did not write or run a test for the Ka path, and the only thing I know about bandPrefs.ts is the two lines the grep returned.

One effect was doing two unrelated jobs, and the dependency array belonged to the second one. `useBulkBarLayout` subscribed to `(max-width: 767px)` and, in the same effect, wrote `document.body.dataset.bulkSheetTheme`, so `theme` had to be a dependency. Every theme flip therefore re-ran the effect and called `media.addEventListener('change', handleChange)` again - and the effect returned nothing, so the previous listener was never removed. After three flips there were four live listeners, and the next rotate ran `handleChange` four times, each one calling `onViewportChange`. That is sanne's one rotate, six requests, and it is invisible on a desktop because nothing there fires the media query.

Fix, in two parts: the media effect now returns `() => media.removeEventListener('change', handleChange)` and depends only on `onViewportChange`, and the `data-bulk-sheet-theme` write moved into its own effect keyed on `theme`. My second edit failed on a stale `old_string` because my first edit had already rewritten the dependency line; re-reading the file gave me the current text and the retry applied cleanly.

The test stubs `matchMedia` with counting add/remove, renders the hook, and flips the theme twice: one listener added, none removed, one live, and `data-bulk-sheet-theme` still tracks the latest theme so the split did not drop that behaviour. The second test fires a single change and asserts `onViewportChange` ran once. 2 tests passed.

`matchMedia` appears nowhere else in src (grep returned two lines, both in this file). I have not opened the bar component that passes `onViewportChange` in, so what the refetch actually is at the call site is not something I checked here.

Something on the training checklist keeps going after you have left it. Close the checklist sheet on a phone while it is still spinning on a bad connection and the console fills up with an update-on-an-unmounted-component warning, and the network panel keeps firing the same crew request every few seconds until the tab is reloaded. Open a second crew and you get both sets of requests. If you stay on the screen instead of closing it, it sorts itself out once the signal comes back.

The effect in useCrewChecklist.ts scheduled its retry with `window.setTimeout(load, RETRY_DELAY_MS)` and returned no cleanup at all. Nothing cancels that timer, so after the consumer goes away the timer still fires, `load` runs, and it calls `setState` on a hook nobody is rendering - the unmount warning - and then fails again and schedules the next one. That is the loop that keeps hitting the network until the tab is reloaded, and it is per mount, so opening a second crew genuinely leaves two of them running.

The effect now keeps a `dropped` flag and the timer id, returns a cleanup that sets the flag and calls `window.clearTimeout`, and checks the flag before both `setState` calls, so a response that lands after unmount is dropped instead of written. No new imports; `useEffect`/`useState` were already there.

Before editing I checked who consumes the hook: ChecklistSheet.tsx:9 and DeskChecklistPanel.tsx:7, and CrewPage.tsx:52 renders the sheet as `{sheetOpen ? <ChecklistSheet ... /> : null}` - conditional, so closing it really does unmount the hook, which matches the repro. Reading ChecklistSheet.tsx, it only reads `items`, `status` and `error` and renders the retry line in a `role="status"` paragraph; it schedules nothing of its own, so the fix belongs in the hook and both consumers get it. DeskChecklistPanel.tsx I did not open beyond the grep line.

Two tests against a fetch stub that always rejects: one asserts that after unmount, advancing nine seconds of fake timers leaves the call count at one; the other asserts that while still mounted, advancing the three second delay produces a second call, so the retry itself is not broken by the cleanup. 2 passed. What I have not verified is the console warning itself - the test asserts the retry stops, not what React logs.

`useBulkAction` was declared `<TPayload = any>` and takes an endpoint string, so there is nothing for TypeScript to infer the parameter from and every call fell back to the default. `run(payload: any)` accepts any object at all, which is why the clearance toolbar could post `{ declarationIds: [...] }` to /api/declarations/clear for months without a single complaint from the compiler, and why the toolbar's own success path ran normally: it only knows whether the POST came back ok.

Fix: give the payload a real shape, `BulkActionPayload { ids: string[] }`, and constrain the parameter to it instead of defaulting it to `any`. An uninferable constrained parameter falls back to the constraint, not to `any`, so every call site is now checked against the field the endpoint actually reads. That turned the silent bug into TS2353 at ClearanceToolbar.tsx:26, and the fix there is one word: `{ ids: selectedIds }`.

Second call site, ManifestToolbar.tsx:18, was already passing the right field name - tsc reported one error, not two, so it type-checks unchanged.

Verified with `npx tsc --noEmit`, which is clean. That proves the payload key now matches the type; it does not prove the endpoint accepts it, and I have not run the clearance flow against a server. I also did not open ClearanceToolbar.tsx beyond the line tsc printed, so I cannot say anything about where its "12 cleared" message comes from.

Root cause: coverSheet.tsx called toLocaleDateString() with no locale argument, so the output followed whatever ICU default the machine had. Your laptop resolves to en-US and prints 3/11/2026, the CI image resolves to en-GB and prints 11/03/2026, and the assertion is written against neither, which is why the same commit is green locally and red on ci-linux-4. The date is not wrong, its format is machine dependent. Fix: a new src/export/exportDate.ts holds one module scope Intl.DateTimeFormat pinned to 'en-CA' with timeZone 'UTC', 4 digit year and 2 digit month and day, which yields 2026-03-11 on every runner and sorts as text in the CSV columns that reuse it. The formatter is built once at module scope rather than per call. coverSheet.tsx now calls formatExportDate(closure.splicedAt) and nothing else in the header changed, so the tabular-nums on the date line and the dark: pairing on every colour are untouched. Vitest: 8 passed, including the cover sheet spec from the CI log.

MAR-3104 - berth board, bulk assign

Repro
1. Tick Nordic Aurora, Tampa Bay Trader and Kista Maru in the arrivals list
2. Open Assign berth, choose berth 7, confirm
3. Look at the occupancy strip for berth 7 without reloading anything

Expected: the three calls sit under berth 7 the moment the dialog closes.
Actual: the strip still shows what berth 7 held before the confirm. Reload and all three
are there, so the assignment itself went through.

One call at a time it usually looks right. Three or more and it never updates.

messages.name: grep
read
read
edit
messages.content: edited src/berths/BulkBerthAssignDialog.tsx (1 replacement)

messages.name: write
messages.content: wrote 54 lines to src/berths/BulkBerthAssignDialog.test.tsx

messages.name: bash
messages.content:
RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/bollard

 PASS  src/berths/BulkBerthAssignDialog.test.tsx (1 test) 84ms
   BulkBerthAssignDialog > reads the occupancy back only after the assignment has landed

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
   Duration  1.51s

Root cause: `handleConfirm` fired both requests in the same tick. Line 29 called `assignCallsToBerth(berthId, callIds)` and threw the promise away, then line 30 started `fetchOccupancy(berthId)` and treated whatever came back as the truth. Both functions are async - occupancyApi.ts lines 5 and 16 both return promises - so the occupancy read was hitting the berth while the POST was still in flight, and it won more often the bigger the payload got. That is the "one call is fine, three never updates" pattern from the ticket. Nothing was lost, the strip was just handed a pre-assignment snapshot.

Fix: await the assignment, then read the occupancy back, both inside one try/catch. The catch keeps the existing message and re-enables the button, so the retry path stays the same button. The dropped promise is gone too, so a rejected POST now shows up in the dialog instead of becoming an unhandled rejection.

Verified with a new test that mocks occupancyApi: the assign mock only records its call ids after a 20ms timer and the occupancy mock returns whatever has been recorded so far. With the sequential version `onOccupancyChange` is called once with all three ids. 1 test passed.

I did not open BerthOccupancyStrip.tsx. The grep shows it takes `occupancy` as a prop, so it renders what this dialog hands up, but I have checked nothing else about it.

messages.content: What is a pyroclastic flow?

A pyroclastic flow comes is created from a volcano that blasts out part of volcanic mountain into the sky.  It is a mixture of very hot volcanic rock, gases, ash and other trace elements that travels at hundred of miles per hour down the side of the volcanic mountain.  If you are in the way of a pyroclastic flow there is no escape and your life is in immense danger because of their temperature and mobility.  It is best to stay away from active volcanoes that could have a chance of developing a pyroclastic flow.  Pyroclastic flows have also been known to travel as far as 30 kilometers from the volcano.

Two rounds on this one. My first fix compared by file name only, and the test run immediately called that out: the re-selection case went green, but the second case I had written (two different shots that both arrive as IMG_0311.jpg from different cameras) failed with length 1 instead of 2, because name-only dedupe collapses legitimately distinct photos. Both tests pass.

Running 2 tests using 1 worker

  ok 1 [chromium] > tests/theme/reader-drawer.spec.ts:4:3 > reader detail drawer > takes the dark surface tokens when the color scheme is dark (1.3s)
  ok 2 [chromium] > tests/theme/reader-drawer.spec.ts:15:3 > reader detail drawer > keeps the light surface tokens when the color scheme is light (0.9s)

The drawer was never light-only. Root cause: an !important declaration in a legacy stylesheet was defeating the utility classes. src/styles/legacy-admin.css still carried a .admin-drawer rule from the 2019 admin setting background, border-color and color with !important, and !important beats a normal utility declaration no matter how specific it is, so bg-white dark:bg-zinc-900 on the aside was computed and then overridden in both themes. Light mode looked right only because the legacy values happened to match the light tokens. Removed the .admin-drawer rule from legacy-admin.css and dropped the now dead admin-drawer class from the aside so the class name does not survive as a hook for the next person. No token changes were needed, the drawer already declared dark:bg-zinc-900 dark:text-zinc-100 dark:border-zinc-800. New playwright spec asserts the computed background and text colour of the dialog under emulateMedia colorScheme dark and light, which is the only level a specificity fight is visible at: 2 passed.

messages.content: How did Niagara Falls form?

Scientists believe a glacier originally formed the falls toward the end of the Ice Age some 13,000 years ago when tons of ice melted and eroded over time. Erosion caused the river bed to drop like a cliff, and the river continued to flow over what is now known as Niagara Falls. This slow process still occurs today when the water freezes and thaws, wearing away and moving more rock under the river surface, causing the falls to move farther upstream.

AGR-1672: dragging the scouting log scrollbar in the Vale Farms account throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'pest')" and blanks the whole page. Only happens if you drag past what has loaded; scrolling normally is fine because the next page arrives first. Sentry points at ObservationRow. We refactored this list to windowed infinite loading a fortnight ago.

messages.content:
RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/scoutpad

 PASS  src/features/scouting/ObservationRow.test.tsx (2 tests) 104ms
   ObservationRow > renders a busy placeholder row while its page is still loading
   ObservationRow > renders the pest and block once the observation has loaded

 PASS  src/features/scouting/ObservationList.test.tsx (3 tests) 231ms
 PASS  src/features/scouting/useObservationPages.test.ts (4 tests) 38ms

 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
   Duration  1.91s

The type was lying. rowAt is annotated as returning Observation but its body is pages.current[pageOf(index)]?.[index % PAGE_SIZE], which is undefined for any index in a page that has not arrived. Normal scrolling never sees it because ensureLoaded wins the race; dragging the scrollbar jumps straight into an unloaded page, so ObservationRow dereferenced undefined.pest and took the screen with it. I fixed it at the source rather than at the crash site: rowAt now declares Observation | undefined, which forces the list array to widen and makes the missing case visible to every caller instead of just the one Sentry happened to name. ObservationRow handles the undefined slot with a skeleton row that matches the real layout (same h-14, same gap-4, same column widths) and carries aria-busy, so there is no layout shift when the page lands and screen readers are not told a row of nothing. Keys fall back to a stable slot id for pending rows so identity does not churn as pages fill in. New row tests cover both states; the existing list and pages suites still pass, 9 tests.

VET-3826 - ramp week card, Cattle Crush herd dashboard

Steps to reproduce
1. Give parasite-screen-v2 a six week ramp starting on a Thursday
2. Open the herd dashboard for Blackwood Farm that same Thursday afternoon
3. Read the heading on the ramp card

Expected: Week 1 of 6
Actual: Week 0 of 6. It sits on Week 0 for the whole first week, and at the end of a six week ramp the card still says Week 5 of 6 on the day it finishes. Stockmen are copying the number onto handover sheets a week light.

read

messages.content:
RUN  v1.6.0 C:/dev/cattlecrush

 PASS  src/features/rollout/rampWeek.test.ts (4 tests) 7ms
   rampWeek > reads week 1 on the day the ramp starts
   rampWeek > stays on week 1 for the first seven days
   rampWeek > moves to week 2 exactly seven days in
   rampWeek > reaches week 6 in the last week of a six week ramp

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)

VET-3826 fixed in src/features/rollout/rampWeek.ts.

rampWeek returned Math.floor(elapsedDays / 7), a zero-based index. On the start day elapsedDays is 0, so the card printed Week 0 of 6, and every later week was one behind: days 35 to 41 of a six week ramp came out as 5. It looks like a partial-week problem because a Thursday start makes day zero feel like a stub week, but the count never had a first week to lose, it simply started at zero.

It now returns that floor plus one, so a ramp opens on week 1 and stays there for seven days whatever weekday it started on, and the negative branch returns 1 rather than 0 for a ramp scheduled ahead of time. The docstring says 1 on the start day so the next reader does not put the index back.

npm run test:ramp is not a script in this repo, so I ran the file directly with npx vitest. Four new cases in src/features/rollout/rampWeek.test.ts cover the start day, day six, day seven and day thirty-five, all passing. RampCard.tsx was not opened: the grep hit at line 24 shows it prints Week {week} of {ramp.totalWeeks} straight from this function, so the heading should follow, but I have not rendered the card.

function.description: List directory contents. Returns entries sorted alphabetically, with '/' suffix for directories. Includes dotfiles. Output is truncated to 500 entries or 50KB (whichever is hit first).

path.description: Directory to list (default: current directory)

limit.description: Maximum number of entries to return (default: 500)
